items.descriptionOriginal: The GPS on your phone helps you find your way to a favourite restaurant, avoid traffic jams and take an unfamiliar road with confidence. It tells you where you are and helps you figure out where to go next . Now, imagine a similar guiding system inside an operating theatre, helping a surgeon navigate the delicate structures of the human brain or spine. That is the idea behind easyNav , an image-guided surgical navigation system developed by Bengaluru-based health-tech company HRS Navigation. Using medical images to map a patient's anatomy and track surgical instruments in real time, the technology helps surgeons understand where they are operating, particularly when working around sensitive nerves, blood vessels, and other critical structures. Founded in 2015 by Arpit Paliwal and Shweta Paliwal, HRS Navigation has developed an indigenous alternative to imported surgical navigation platforms. Its systems are now installed in more than 200 hospitals and have supported over 20,000 surgeries, according to the company. Using CT scans, easyNav creates a map of the patient's anatomy and tracks surgical instruments in real time. But the motivation behind the startup was not simply to build sophisticated medical technology. It was to address a question that Arpit encountered repeatedly: why should access to advanced surgical care depend so heavily on where a patient lives or how much they can afford? Why surgical precision needed to reach beyond metros An electronics engineer who also completed an executive programme at IIM Calcutta, Arpit spent around 11 years in an international role before deciding to build a medical technology company in India. His experience had given him an understanding of surgical navigation and the standards these systems needed to meet. It had also helped him recognise a gap in the market. Surgical navigation technology was already available internationally, but its adoption in India was constrained by more than the cost of purchasing a machine. Some imported systems required hospitals to buy recurring consumables for every procedure or upgrade their operating theatres to meet specific infrastructure requirements. For hospitals working with limited budgets, these expenses could make the technology difficult to sustain, particularly when treating patients who could not afford to pay much for surgery. Arpit recalls meeting families who were struggling to afford treatment. One interaction that stayed with him was that of a father who told him to proceed with his child's operation, saying he would sell his house to arrange the money. Surgical navigation helps doctors locate tumours and understand their proximity to critical nerves, blood vessels and other structures. "I have seen that kind of reality," he says, describing the experiences that motivated him to build something for India. For him, the problem was not a lack of medical expertise. It was that the tools available to support complex procedures were not always accessible to the hospitals and patients who needed them. Simply reducing the price of an imported system would not necessarily solve this problem . The technology also had to work within the realities of Indian hospitals. "You need to adapt your system to work with the requirements of Indian infrastructure," Arpit explains. That became a guiding principle for HRS Navigation. Starting with a small office and building its technology from the ground up, the founders set out to develop a system that could work with the equipment hospitals already had, without compromising on accuracy. It was a demanding undertaking in a field requiring extensive research, engineering, testing and regulatory compliance. Arpit says developing the technology from the prototype stage took years of work, including studying research papers and building the team's technical expertise at a time when many of today's AI tools were not available. The effort eventually led to easyNav , designed around two priorities: precision that meets demanding clinical requirements and adaptability that makes the system practical for Indian hospitals. How does a GPS for surgeons work? To understand the technology, consider what happens when someone drives through an unfamiliar city without navigation. They must rely on signboards, landmarks and their own judgement to decide which road to take. A GPS adds another layer of information, showing their position in relation to the route and helping them correct their direction as they move. Surgical navigation applies a comparable principle inside the operating theatre, using medical imaging rather than road maps. Before surgery, CT scans provide detailed images of the patient's anatomy. These images are used to create a reference for the procedure. During the operation, the navigation system tracks the position of surgical instruments and displays where they are in relation to that anatomy. HRS Navigation designed easyNav to work with existing operating theatre infrastructure, making adoption easier for hospitals. This gives the surgeon an additional way to check the instrument's position and trajectory, particularly when the target lies deep inside the body or close to structures that must be preserved. In brain surgery, for instance, the system can help a surgeon plan the route to a tumour and understand its relationship with important structures. In spine procedures, it can help determine the entry point and trajectory for placing screws. Dr Ranjit Deshmukh, consultant neurosurgeon at Sahyadri Hospital, Pune, explains that complex procedures have traditionally relied on anatomical landmarks, surgical experience and imaging during the operation to establish orientation. "Navigation provides an additional layer of anatomical guidance, helping the surgeon plan and execute these procedures with greater confidence ," he says. With easyNav , Dr Deshmukh says he can understand where his instruments are in relation to the patient's anatomy in real time. He particularly values this in complex brain surgeries involving deep-seated tumours, lesions near major blood vessels and procedures around the skull base. The technology can also support planning when a tumour lies close to functional areas of the brain. Information from techniques such as functional MRI and tractography can help surgeons understand these relationships and plan an approach that aims to remove as much of the tumour as safely possible while preserving critical functions. Importantly, navigation does not replace a surgeon's judgement or experience. Instead, it provides additional information to support decisions during critical stages of an operation. Dr Deshmukh says he has used international navigation platforms for around 15 years and finds easyNav comparable in ease of use and overall workflow. "Once a surgical team becomes familiar with the system, it integrates into the procedure without adding unnecessary complexity," he adds. easyNav uses CT scans to create a 3D map of a patient's anatomy and infrared cameras to track surgical instruments in real time. He has also noticed a reduction in uncertainty during many complex cases, although he cautions that complications and revision rates depend on several factors and cannot be attributed to a single technology. For Arpit, maintaining this precision while making the system affordable required extensive research into components, performance, and design. The team worked to meet international quality and regulatory parameters while developing a system suited to the infrastructure and needs of its intended users. From a small-town hospital to a mother's second chance The value of this approach becomes clearer when the technology reaches hospitals beyond major metropolitan centres. Arpit recalls a surgeon in a small town in Maharashtra who used the system to operate on a young child from a farming family. The family had limited financial resources, and the surgeon operated for around Rs 10,000. When the surgeon shared the outcome with colleagues, they were surprised that such a procedure had been performed at a small centre. For Arpit, this was precisely the kind of change HRS Navigation had hoped to enable: helping skilled doctors access tools that can support complex surgery, even outside the largest hospitals. Another example comes from a trust hospital in Siddhagiri, Maharashtra, where the system has been in use for several years. According to Arpit, patients travel there from Maharashtra and neighbouring Karnataka because the hospital offers treatment at affordable rates. He recalls the case of a mother of three who had a brain tumour in a particularly difficult location. After approaching several larger hospitals, she eventually underwent surgery at the trust hospital. The procedure was successful, and she survived with her neurological functions preserved, Arpit says. Stories such as these illustrate why surgical navigation can matter beyond the operating theatre. When a hospital can offer complex procedures at an affordable cost, patients may have another option closer to home instead of having to travel to a major city. Surgical navigation can help patients access complex procedures closer to home, without travelling to larger cities. The impact is not limited to patients, either. Surgeons can gain confidence from being able to verify their instruments' positions during difficult procedures. Arpit recalls how some senior surgeons initially questioned the system when its guidance differed from their expectations. After repeatedly checking its accuracy during operations, he says many began relying on it as an important part of their workflow. The company also points to a memorable procedure in Guntur in which a patient undergoing brain surgery remained awake and watched the film Baahubali . Unlike most brain surgeries, which are performed under general anaesthesia, an awake craniotomy requires the patient to remain conscious so doctors can monitor essential brain functions in real time. In this case, the patient was comfortable enough to watch a film while the surgical team monitored his responses using HRS Navigation's technology. "The case attracted widespread media attention," Arpit says. For the team, the procedure was a memorable demonstration of how image-guided technology can support surgeons in carefully selected operations where monitoring a patient's core functions is essential. HRS Navigation's systems are now used across a wide range of hospitals, from smaller centres in places such as Guntur and Gorakhpur to larger institutions, including Apollo hospitals and AIIMS facilities. Dr Deshmukh believes such technologies can help narrow the gap between metro and non-metro healthcare facilities, provided hospitals also have the clinical expertise, training and technical support needed to use them effectively. "Advanced surgical technologies should not be limited to a few tertiary centres in major cities," he says. Building medical technology in India, for the world Making precision technology accessible also means rethinking the business model behind it. Arpit says HRS Navigation has avoided recurring consumable costs for every procedure, a model he believes can help hospitals use the system without having to weigh the expense of additional supplies against a patient's ability to pay. The company has also designed easyNav to work with existing operating theatre infrastructure, reducing the need for hospitals to make extensive changes before adopting the technology. These decisions are part of a larger ambition: to demonstrate that sophisticated medical devices can be designed and built in India without compromising on performance. Arpit says HRS Navigation has received international recognition for its product design, including an iF Design Award from Germany and an A' Design Award from Italy. The company has also been selected by India's Department of Science and Technology for recognition linked to the country's 75 years of independence. For him, these milestones matter because medical technology made in India should be judged on what it can achieve, rather than assumptions about where it comes from. "We have taken a long path of doing it from India," he says, describing the company's ambition to become globally respected. That ambition is closely tied to the reason he started the company in the first place. The goal is not only to compete with established international manufacturers but also to make precision healthcare more accessible to people who might otherwise struggle to reach it. HRS Navigation's systems are now installed in over 200 hospitals and have supported more than 20,000 surgeries. Surgical navigation cannot, on its own, solve every challenge in healthcare. The right equipment must work alongside skilled surgeons, trained teams, reliable support and hospitals that patients can afford to access. "But when those pieces come together, technology can expand what a hospital is equipped to offer and give surgeons another tool to make informed decisions," adds Arpit. For the family trying to afford an operation, the surgeon working in a smaller town, or the patient who needs a complex procedure without travelling hundreds of kilometres, that difference can be deeply personal. And that is the promise behind HRS Navigation's homegrown GPS for surgeons: not simply helping doctors find their way through the human body, but helping more patients find their way to advanced surgical care. items.descriptionOriginal: Sewage is full of organic matter that can be a source of energy. But it also carries harmful chemicals as well as leftover medicines that conventional treatment methods can’t remove easily. Researchers now report a technology that can solve three sewage-related problems at the same time. Their new device uses bacteria in wastewater to generate electricity while breaking down a hard-to-degrade antibiotic and producing a valuable industrial chemical. The team published their results in Journal of Power Sources . There have been plenty of research efforts to harness microbes for treating wastewater while producing renewable energy. The approach uses microbial fuel cells , which are battery-like devices with two electrodes. In microbial fuel cells, bacteria grow on an electrode and devour organic matter , converting chemical energy into electrons, which flow in an external circuit to produce electricity. Then those electrons meet oxygen at the other electrode to create water. Turns out that microbial fuel cells usually generate very small amounts of electricity. “So we asked a different question: What else could those electrons do when they arrive?,” writes the team from both;} Recommended Reading: Designer bacteria clean wastewater and generate power—at the same time If all the electrons don’t combine with oxygen and hydrogen at the second electrode, the product is hydrogen peroxide instead of water. Hydrogen peroxide is a household chemical used for disinfection and bleaching. It is also used widely in chemical manufacturing. The chemical industry makes it today using an energy- and chemical-intensive process in large plants. To get the right reaction in the microbial fuel cell, the researchers designed a new electrode. They embedded iron and nickel oxides on a flexible carbon fiber cloth. When they heated the cloth in the presence of acetylene at 800°C, a forest of carbon nanofibers grew out of it. “The metal particles rode the growing fibers upward, so every fiber ended with a metal oxide tip,” the researchers say. So the electrode has conductive fibers with a catalytic tip. And bacteria cling to this rough conductive surface and form a thick film. The team used the same electrodes on both side of the fuel cell. When they ran sewage spiked with the antibiotic chloramphenicol through the cell, it removed 99.99% of the drug while producing hydrogen peroxide in two days. “Next, we plan to run it longer, test other drugs, check the toxicity of the breakdown products and link several cells in series to raise the power,” the team writes. “So can dirty water help pay for its own cleanup? Not completely yet. But in two days, our system turned sewage into cleaner water, a useful chemical and a little electricity.” Source : Yashmeen Budania et al. items.descriptionOriginal: In 1995, Professor Sekhar Raghavan noticed something unusual about the water coming from his tap in Chennai. It had turned salty. As groundwater levels fell, seawater was seeping into the city's underground freshwater reserves, making the water increasingly difficult to use. The problem was not that Chennai received too little rain. The city received substantial rainfall, but much of it flowed through roads and drains into the sea instead of replenishing the groundwater beneath its homes. For Raghavan, this raised a question. If the rain was falling over the city, why was so little of it being saved? His answer was to take rainwater harvesting to the people. Armed with a bicycle and a simple message, he began visiting neighbourhoods, going from door to door to convince residents to collect rainwater and direct it back into the ground. Nearly three decades later, his campaign offers a lesson to another Indian city struggling with water scarcity: Hyderabad. When the rain falls, but the wells run dry Home to around 1.5 crore people, the city is grappling with an acute drinking water shortage driven by uneven regional water availability, competing agricultural and industrial demand, and a monsoon deficit. More than 330 of Telangana's 600-plus mandals have been classified as drought-hit, while only around 500 of the state's 6,000-plus lakes have water, according to data shared by the state irrigation department. The pressure is visible in the city's growing dependence on tankers . Daily bookings have surged to between 6,000 and 8,000, prompting Hyderabad Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board Managing Director Ashok Reddy to direct officials to onboard additional tanker operators and begin their registration. In parts of Secunderabad Cantonment and Hyderabad's outskirts, residents have reported receiving drinking water only once every three to four days. One of the city's main reservoirs has also reportedly fallen to around 13% of its capacity. But the shortage is not only about how much water a city receives. It is also about how much it can retain. That is where Chennai's experience becomes relevant. One bicycle, one neighbourhood at a time When Raghavan began his campaign in 1995, rainwater harvesting was not a familiar practice among most urban households. He set out to change that, explaining how rainwater collected from rooftops, driveways and other surfaces could be filtered and directed into recharge structures, allowing it to seep into the soil and replenish underground aquifers. Instead of allowing rainwater to run off into drains, households could capture it and help restore the groundwater they depended on. However, convincing people was harder than explaining the science. Raghavan cycled through neighbourhoods, speaking to residents and encouraging them to install harvesting systems. Many initially dismissed the idea, but he continued working with communities to demonstrate how it could be done. Through the Rain Centre, which he led, he also worked with a team of plumbers and well-diggers to survey systems across the city and demonstrate rainwater harvesting through model houses. How Chennai turned an idea into a law In October 2002, the Tamil Nadu government enacted legislation to make rainwater harvesting compulsory. An ordinance followed in June 2003, extending the requirement to all existing buildings across the state, including Chennai. Property owners were required to install systems by 11 October, 2003. Non-compliance could invite penalties, including fines or disconnection of government water supply. The government's November 2003 announcement reported that 99.5% of Chennai's residents had implemented rainwater harvesting in their houses and apartment complexes. But installing a system and making it work are two different things. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) A Rain Centre survey conducted in a residential colony between October and November 2003 found that around half the residents had implemented rainwater harvesting unsatisfactorily. Even among those who had installed systems correctly, many focused only on collecting rooftop rainwater. They overlooked another important source: the rain falling across the rest of their premises. In apartment complexes, this surface runoff could amount to twice or more the volume collected from rooftops. Although this water may not be suitable for direct household use, it can still be directed into the soil to replenish groundwater. As it moves through the soil, natural filtration helps remove contaminants. The missing piece: What happens beyond the rooftop? Raghavan's work also highlighted a larger gap in Chennai's approach. While households had a responsibility to harvest rainwater within their properties, public spaces presented another opportunity. Roads, parks and playgrounds receive considerable rainfall. Yet much of the water flowing through Chennai's stormwater drains is channelled towards the city's waterwys and eventually discharged into the Bay of Bengal. Instead of allowing all this runoff to escape, the Rain Centre advocated directing suitable urban runoff into recharge structures. This, however, requires careful planning. Road runoff carries solid waste, fine silt and other contaminants that can clog harvesting structures. Systems must therefore account for filtration, waste removal and regular maintenance. In parts of Secunderabad Cantonment and Hyderabad's outskirts, residents have reported receiving drinking water only once every three to four days. Photograph: (Representational image-Aijaz Rahi/AP Photo) The city also needs adequate open spaces and appropriately designed recharge structures to prevent stagnant water and flooding. In other words, collecting rainwater is only one part of managing it. What Chennai's experience tells Hyderabad The results of Chennai's efforts became more visible after the rains returned. Tamil Nadu received below-average rainfall in 2003 and 2004, making the immediate benefits difficult for residents to see. The following year brought heavier rainfall, offering a clearer demonstration of what functioning harvesting systems could achieve. After the 2005 rains, the Rain Centre observed groundwater levels rising by around 20 feet in areas it monitored, encouraging the team to continue its work. For nearly 15 years, rainwater harvesting helped Chennai strengthen its groundwater reserves . However, the city's 2019 water crisis exposed the limitations of relying on infrastructure that was no longer adequately maintained. Clogged filters, neglected recharge pits, and poorly functioning systems weakened the impact of the original initiative. Today, Chennai is exploring additional approaches, including sponge parks and underground rainwater capture systems, to improve its capacity to retain rainfall. For Hyderabad, the lesson is not simply to replicate Chennai's legislation or install harvesting structures across buildings . It is to build a system in which households, communities and civic authorities share responsibility for capturing rainwater, maintaining recharge structures and protecting groundwater. Raghavan's journey began with a salty tap and a bicycle. What followed was a citywide conversation that helped turn an overlooked resource into an urban water-management priority. items.descriptionOriginal: On 5 November, Delhi's Air Quality Index (AQI) reached 370 , placing the capital in the very poor category. At Jahangirpuri, the reading climbed to 459, entering the severe category. As winter settles over northern India, the familiar response is to increase road sweeping, sprinkle water and intensify construction-site inspections. Yet there is a problem with the way cities clean their roads. A street can look spotless while fine particles escape into the air. Vehicles can then lift the remaining dust again, exposing pedestrians, cyclists and residents to pollution. The question is not simply whether municipalities should sweep more often, but whether they can remove dust without making it airborne. Three Indian cities offer different answers . Lucknow has expanded mechanised sweeping, Parwanoo has focused on repairing the surfaces that generate dust, and Chandigarh is testing a method that combines treated-water washing with mechanical cleaning. Together, their experiences show why cleaner roads require more than a broom. Lucknow takes cleaning beyond the broom In September 2026, Lucknow won the top position in the Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan among cities with populations exceeding 10 lakh. Its Ward 70, in Zone 4, also ranked first nationally among wards with more than 30,000 residents. The recognition followed a citywide effort to tackle several sources of pollution, including road dust, vehicle emissions and waste burning. Loose soil and debris along road shoulders can be repeatedly disturbed by traffic, making roadside maintenance an important part of dust control. Photograph: ( Hindustan Times ) The Lucknow Municipal Corporation deployed 97 electric mechanised sweeping machines. These machines use rotating brushes to collect debris, while suction systems can help capture finer material instead of simply pushing it aside. The city also paved approximately 559.85 km of roads end-to-end, reducing exposed surfaces that passing vehicles can disturb. Officials said the combination of mechanised sweeping and paving helped control resuspended road dust. The ward-level recognition is particularly significant because air pollution is experienced locally. A city may have an ambitious clean-air plan , but residents encounter its results on the street outside their homes. Ward 70's achievement shows how clean-air action can be assessed at a neighbourhood level. However, the award does not establish how much pollution the ward's individual interventions reduced. The challenge is to translate recognition into sustained, measurable improvements in the air residents breathe. Parwanoo fixes the road that creates the dust In Parwanoo, a town in Himachal Pradesh, officials began by asking a different question: what if the road itself was generating the dust? Damaged road surfaces, crumbling edges and poorly managed construction waste can all contribute to the dust that settles on urban streets. Photograph: ( TOI ) An IIT Kanpur study covering the town's 8.5 sq km identified road dust as a major source of air pollution . The municipal response focused on repairing the surfaces and conditions that allowed dust to accumulate. A 9 km stretch of road was upgraded with paver blocks and interlocking tiles, replacing crumbling surfaces. Drainage systems were improved to prevent erosion, while construction and demolition waste came under closer scrutiny. The town also developed a 0.27-acre green buffer zone, intensified plantation efforts, and curbed open garbage dumping. The outcome was measurable. Parwanoo's annual average PM10 concentration fell from 66 micrograms per cubic metre in 2017-18 to 39 micrograms per cubic metre in 2023-24, a reduction of about 41%. PM10 refers to particles with a diameter of 10 micrometres or less. Road dust can contain these particles, which can enter the respiratory system. The reduction cannot be attributed to paving alone. Parwanoo's efforts included several interventions, and the town's experience demonstrates the value of addressing dust at its source rather than relying exclusively on cleaning after it has accumulated. Chandigarh tests whether washing can help Chandigarh is approaching the problem through a pilot project. In September 2025, the Chandigarh Pollution Control Committee directed officials to launch a dust-control initiative on a dust-prone road corridor. The plan combined road washing with treated water, mechanised sweeping and cleaning of road shoulders. Road dust contains PM10 particles, which measure 10 micrometres or less in diameter and can enter the respiratory system. Photograph: ( HT ) Road shoulders matter because loose soil and debris along the edges can be repeatedly disturbed by vehicles. Cleaning only the central carriageway can leave a substantial source of dust untouched. The committee planned to monitor PM10 levels during the pilot and use the findings to decide whether the intervention could be expanded across the city. The project also sits within a wider effort to control construction and demolition waste. Authorities directed institutions and agencies to suppress dust at stockyards, cover loose soil with vegetation and use sprinklers or anti-smog guns where appropriate. The distinction is important: Chandigarh's project was announced as a pilot, not a proven citywide success. Its value lies in testing whether road washing and mechanical cleaning can work together, and whether air-quality monitoring can establish their effectiveness. What Delhi can learn Delhi's pollution is not caused by road dust alone. Vehicle emissions, industrial activity, construction, waste burning, agricultural fires and winter weather conditions all contribute to the city's air-quality episodes. But that does not make road dust control insignificant. It makes targeted interventions more important. Lucknow demonstrates the value of mechanised cleaning and neighbourhood-level action. Parwanoo shows why repairing damaged roads and controlling construction waste can prevent dust from accumulating. Chandigarh is testing whether treated-water washing and shoulder cleaning can improve the results. The larger lesson is that road cleaning should not be measured only by the amount of dust collected or the number of machines deployed. Road dust control works best when cities prevent loose particles from returning to the air, making cleaner streets a practical step towards healthier urban environments. Photograph: ( The Indian Express ) Municipalities need to measure how much dust remains on roads, how quickly it returns, and whether particulate pollution declines. For a city like Delhi, where winter pollution can become a public-health emergency, cleaner roads are not a complete solution. But they are a tangible civic intervention that can be planned, monitored, and improved. The real test of a clean road is not how it looks after a sweeping vehicle passes. It is how much dust stays out of the air afterwards. Sources ' Lucknow is known for traffic and dust. How did it top India's clean-air ranking? items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Protecting Forests from Disturbance Outperforms Restoration for Amazon Biodiversity, Study Finds Reading Time: 3 minutes Across 3 million hectares of the Brazilian Amazon, protecting forests from disturbance delivered greater biodiversity benefits than restoring already-cleared land, according to new research comparing conservation strategies. Conservation policy has long debated where limited funding should go: preventing deforestation outright, protecting standing forests from degradation, or restoring land already cleared. A study published in Science this September provides the clearest answer yet, using counterfactual scenarios built from observed land-use changes across three million hectares of the Brazilian Amazon’s deforestation frontier. Led by Leonardo S. Miranda of Lancaster University alongside researchers including Joice Ferreira of Embrapa, the team compared three intervention types against what actually happened on the ground. Protecting forests from disturbance, meaning avoiding fire and selective logging within standing forest, reduced biodiversity loss by 68.5% and carbon loss by 46.8% compared with the baseline scenario. Avoiding deforestation entirely mitigated 60.8% of carbon loss and 28.0% of biodiversity loss. Restoration of already-cleared land delivered the smallest gains for both outcomes. These findings challenge a common assumption in conservation funding, where restoration often receives outsized attention and investment despite standing forests requiring protection first. Protecting forests from disturbance proved nearly as effective as preventing deforestation for carbon storage, while substantially outperforming it for biodiversity outcomes, a distinction with direct implications for how governments and conservation organizations allocate resources. Neither single intervention alone reversed losses across the landscape. Combining avoided deforestation with protection from disturbance was necessary to achieve net-positive outcomes, increasing biodiversity by 12% and carbon by 18% above 2010 baseline levels. This combined approach proved essential precisely because deforestation and forest degradation operate through different mechanisms, requiring complementary rather than substitutable responses. Restoration still carries genuine value, particularly in landscapes where deforestation has already progressed extensively. The research team found that restoration delivered meaningful benefits, particularly on properties where much of the original forest cover had already disappeared, suggesting it works best as a complement to protection rather than a replacement. Protecting forests from disturbance addresses threats that often receive less policy attention than outright deforestation. Selective logging removes valuable timber species while leaving forest canopy nominally intact, and wildfires increasingly penetrate forest edges weakened by fragmentation and drought. Both processes degrade forest structure, reduce habitat quality for forest-dependent species, and release stored carbon, yet they generate far less public attention than visible clear-cutting. Protecting forests from disturbance targets fire and selective logging, threats that degrade forest structure without clear-cutting, with researchers finding that combined deforestation and disturbance avoidance are necessary to achieve net-positive biodiversity and carbon outcomes above 2010 baseline levels. Photo by Bill Salazar on Pexels. The study’s timing is especially urgent as climate change intensifies. The research team noted that combined interventions become increasingly important as warming progresses, since forest restoration efforts prove particularly vulnerable to wildfire risk. Newly planted or naturally regenerating young forests lack the structural resilience of mature canopies, making restoration investments vulnerable to being undone by the same fire disturbances the study identifies as critical to prevent. This vulnerability creates a policy challenge extending well beyond Brazil. As governments and international organizations increasingly emphasize forest restoration within climate commitments and biodiversity frameworks, protecting forests from disturbance offers a complementary message: restoration investments achieve far less impact when the remaining standing forest around them continues degrading from fire and logging. Joice Ferreira, principal investigator of the Capoeira restoration research program at Embrapa, emphasized that restoration remains essential precisely where forests have been lost across large areas, reinforcing that the study’s findings don’t diminish restoration’s role but rather clarify where and when it delivers the strongest returns. Restoration works best as part of integrated strategies rather than as a primary tool used independently of forest protection efforts. The research methodology itself offers a template for conservation planning elsewhere. By using observed land-use changes to construct counterfactual scenarios, the team measured what would have happened under different intervention choices and quantified trade-offs that previous studies could only estimate qualitatively. This approach allows policymakers to weigh cost-effectiveness directly rather than relying on intuition about which conservation strategy delivers the greatest return per dollar invested. As tropical deforestation frontiers worldwide face similar pressures from fire, logging, and agricultural expansion, protecting forests from disturbance provides an evidence-based framework extending beyond the Brazilian Amazon alone. The findings suggest that conservation funding achieves maximum impact not through any single strategy in isolation, but through carefully sequenced combinations addressing deforestation, degradation, and restoration simultaneously, each targeting the specific threats most relevant to a given landscape’s current condition. The post Protecting Forests from Disturbance Outperforms Restoration for Amazon Biodiversity, Study Finds appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Every Diwali, the night sky turns into a canvas of colour. Golden fountains of light shoot upwards, flower pots scatter sparkling trails across balconies, and rockets burst into brilliant shades of red, green and blue. For a few hours, the neighbourhood seems to glow with celebration. But when the last spark fades, another side of the festivities begins to show. A cloud of smoke hangs over the streets, the familiar smell of burnt chemicals lingers in the air, and the sound of crackers gives way to coughing, irritated eyes, and difficulty breathing. Firecrackers may last only a few seconds, but the pollution they leave behind can stay in the air much longer. This has led to the growing popularity of an alternative: green crackers. But are they actually better for the environment, and does the word 'green' mean they are safe to burst? What happens when a firecracker goes off? The colourful explosions we enjoy are the result of carefully mixed chemicals that release energy when ignited. But this reaction also releases a cocktail of pollutants into the atmosphere. Conventional firecrackers can emit particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and other harmful gases. These tiny particles can enter the respiratory system, with some travelling deep into the lungs and even entering the bloodstream. For people with asthma , respiratory conditions or heart problems, exposure can make existing symptoms worse. Children and older adults are particularly vulnerable. Even otherwise healthy people may experience coughing, throat irritation, breathlessness and burning eyes. Green crackers use modified chemical formulations designed to reduce particulate emissions compared with conventional fireworks. Photograph: ( Khan Global studies ) There is also the problem of noise pollution. The sudden, loud bursts can cause distress to infants, older people, pets and those sensitive to sound. And when thousands of crackers are burst across a city within a few hours, their emissions add to the pollution already coming from vehicles, industries and other sources. What makes a firecracker green? To address this problem, scientists at the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), along with the National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (NEERI), developed what are known as green crackers. Introduced in India in 2019, these are firecrackers made with modified chemical formulations and reduced quantities of certain raw materials. The idea is simple: retain the familiar sparkle and sound of fireworks while releasing fewer pollutants. Developed by CSIR and NEERI, green crackers fall into three categories: SWAS, STAR and SAFAL, each using a different approach to reduce emissions. Photograph: ( GCESCJ ) According to NEERI's criteria, a green cracker must reduce particulate matter emissions by at least 30% compared with its conventional counterpart. Another qualifying formulation must achieve at least 20% lower particulate emissions, along with a minimum 10% reduction in gaseous emissions such as sulphur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide. The chemistry behind the sparkle So, what actually changes inside these crackers? Scientists work on changing the ingredients, reducing the amount of material used, and making combustion more efficient. There are three recognised categories: SWAS (Safe Water Releaser): These crackers release water vapour during combustion, which helps suppress dust particles and reduce particulate emissions. STAR (Safe Thermite Cracker): These use iron oxide-based formulations to improve combustion efficiency and reduce emissions. SAFAL (Safe Minimal Aluminium): These use zeolite-based materials, which have a porous structure, to help reduce the amount of aluminium required. Green crackers also exclude certain harmful chemicals, including barium nitrate, and use modified formulations to reduce ash and other emissions. Are green crackers completely safe? Here's where the distinction matters: less polluting does not mean pollution-free. Even green crackers release particulate matter and gases when burnt. Some green crackers could release higher numbers of ultrafine particles than conventional ones. These extremely tiny particles are concerning because they can penetrate deep into the respiratory system. This does not mean every green cracker is more harmful, but it shows why simply measuring the total quantity of emissions does not tell the whole story. There is another important point. A 30% reduction in emissions from an individual cracker does not mean the air in a city becomes 30% cleaner. The overall impact depends on how many crackers are burst, the pollutants they release, weather conditions, and other sources of pollution. Green crackers, therefore, are a step towards reducing the damage, not a licence to burst as many as we like. Choosing fewer firecrackers and exploring alternative ways to celebrate can help reduce Diwali's impact on the air we breathe. Photograph: ( The Indian Express ) If buying them, look for products from authorised manufacturers with valid certification rather than trusting packaging that simply says 'eco-friendly' or 'pollution-free' . Perhaps the best way to make Diwali brighter is to think beyond the few seconds a firecracker lights up the sky. Green crackers offer a way to reduce some of the harm, but they cannot take pollution out of the picture entirely. Choosing to burst fewer crackers, exploring other ways to celebrate, and being mindful of the air we all share can make a difference. After all, a festival of lights should leave behind happy memories, not air that makes it harder for people to breathe. Sources: 'Green firecrackers may pollute less, but how clean are they? An expert explains' by Hina Rohtaki for The Indian Express, Published on 31 October 2026. 'EXPLAINED | Green Crackers Allowed for Diwali: What Does 'Green' Really Mean?' by Sunny KS for Open The Magazine

items.descriptionOriginal: Imagine walking through the Western Ghats after the monsoon. The soil is damp, leaves glisten with rain, and tiny saplings grow in the shade of towering trees. Each tree seems to live a life of its own, reaching towards sunlight. Yet beneath your feet, another world is at work. Tiny fungal threads spread through the soil, forming partnerships with tree roots. They help trees find water and nutrients, while the trees provide them with food. Some fungal threads may even connect neighbouring plants. This hidden world has earned a nickname: the 'wood wide web'. But can trees really share resources through it? And what might these underground relationships tell us about protecting forests? The surprising give-and-take beneath tree roots Trees use sunlight to make sugars through photosynthesis. But getting essential nutrients from the ground is another matter. That is where fungi come in. Their microscopic threads reach into tiny spaces in the soil that tree roots cannot easily explore. They help plants take up nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen, and can also improve access to water. In exchange, trees supply the fungi with carbon-rich sugars. Scientists call these partnerships mycorrhizal associations . The name may be unfamiliar, but the arrangement is simple. The fungal threads, known as hyphae , can spread through soil to form a larger web called mycelium . Some fungi associate with several plants at once, potentially linking their roots in what researchers call common mycorrhizal networks . The links are intriguing. What is less certain is whether they regularly allow one tree to support another. Fungi extend through the soil as microscopic filaments called hyphae. Collectively, these filaments form a network known as mycelium. Photograph: (Kabir Gabriel Peay; Advanced Science News) How scientists began mapping the wood wide web In 2019, an international team of researchers, including scientists from Stanford University and ETH Zurich, set out to understand where different tree-fungus partnerships occur around the world. They analysed records from more than 1.1 million forest plots across over 70 countries, covering upwards of 28,000 tree species. With the help of computer models, they mapped the distribution of major types of tree-root partnerships, including those involving fungi and nitrogen-fixing bacteria. The study, published in Nature , showed that these relationships vary with climate. In cooler regions, for instance, the way dead leaves and other organic matter break down can influence which fungal partners thrive. The findings revealed global patterns beneath the forest floor. They also raised questions about how changes in temperature and rainfall could affect the partnerships on which trees depend. Importantly, the scientists mapped broad patterns of association. They did not trace individual fungal threads linking particular trees. Do older trees help younger ones? Perhaps the most captivating idea linked to the wood wide web is that of a 'mother tree': a large, older tree that nourishes nearby seedlings through shared fungal connections. Picture a tiny sapling struggling for sunlight beneath a thick forest canopy. Studies have found that materials can sometimes move between plants associated with fungal networks. But observing movement does not automatically show that a mature tree deliberately helps a seedling, or that the transfer makes the younger tree healthier. In 2023, researchers reviewed studies of common mycorrhizal networks in Nature Ecology & Evolution . They warned that some popular claims had travelled further than the evidence. In particular, they found no published peer-reviewed evidence that mature trees preferentially send resources or warning signals to their own offspring through these networks. So the underground partnerships are real. The popular picture of forests acting like families that look after one another remains unproven. What happens when forest soil is disturbed? Think of the rainforests of the Western Ghats, the sal forests of central and eastern India, or the mountain forests of the Himalayas. Their climates, soils and trees differ, and so do the organisms living around their roots. The 2019 global study offers clues about where different partnerships might occur. It cannot tell us exactly which trees are connected beneath any particular Indian forest. That is why studying local soils and fungi matters. Forest health depends on far more than what grows above ground. Underground organisms help trees obtain nutrients, support the recycling of organic matter and influence how plants respond to changing conditions. When forests are cleared or soils disturbed, these relationships can be disrupted too. Understanding them could help scientists think more carefully about restoring degraded land and protecting existing forests. The next time you walk among trees, consider the soil beneath them. Hidden there are thousands of living connections, doing essential work even as scientists continue to uncover how they function. Protecting a forest begins with understanding the life we can see, and the life we cannot. Source: 'Stanford researchers map symbiotic relationships between trees and microbes worldwide' : By Stanford Report, Published on 15 May 2019 'Mycorrhizal feedbacks influence global forest structure and diversity' : Published on 19 October 2023

items.descriptionOriginal: For centuries, the sacred groves of Rajasthan were understood as human gifts to nature -- places where belief drew a boundary and the forest was allowed to breathe. But as this essay quietly argues, the order of that story is wrong: people protected a handful of fig trees, and the birds did everything else. The peepal, the banyan, the gular -- three figs that tradition placed beyond the reach of the axe - fed birds through every lean season, and those birds, carrying seeds from across the landscape, built the grove outward from that protected center, generation after generation. "What belief really preserved was a process," the author writes, "a place where the planting could go on undisturbed for centuries." There is something worth sitting with in that realization: that the deepest acts of protection are often for something we cannot fully see, and that what looks like a tree standing alone is, if the birds still come, a forest in the making.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Forest Landscape Restoration in Mozambique Launches in Nampula Province Reading Time: 3 minutes Forest landscape restoration in Mozambique has officially begun in Nampula Province, aiming to restore 500 hectares of Miombo woodland and build local livelihoods. Forest landscape restoration in Mozambique took a major step forward this August with the official launch of a new project in Nampula Province. The initiative pairs the Mozambican government with the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), funded by Swiss Development Cooperation. Its goal is to turn national restoration pledges into work that communities can see on the ground. The launch unfolded over two days in Ribáuè District, starting with a briefing for provincial officials and continuing with a public ceremony. Government representatives, private companies, researchers, and local residents participated. Seedlings planted during the event were handed over to a nearby school, where students will track their growth. IUCN’s country representative in Mozambique described the project as reaching well beyond tree planting. The effort aims to improve land productivity and strengthen household livelihoods alongside ecological recovery. That framing positions forest landscape restoration in Mozambique as much an economic strategy as an environmental one. Over the next four years, the project will focus restoration work on 500 hectares within Ribáuè District. Of that total, 400 hectares will restore Miombo woodland, while the remaining 100 hectares will support agroforestry systems mixing crops with trees. The work contributes to Mozambique’s broader Five-Year Programme target of restoring 52,000 hectares nationwide. That national target also feeds into Mozambique’s international commitments under global restoration initiatives. Countries across Africa have pledged millions of hectares to these efforts over the past decade, though turning pledges into on-the-ground results has often proven difficult. A dedicated project with clear hectare targets and funding attached is meant to help close that gap. Miombo woodland stretches across a huge swath of south-central Africa, from Angola to Tanzania and across much of Mozambique. The ecosystem stores significant amounts of carbon and supports roughly half of Africa’s remaining elephant population. Millions of rural households also depend on it directly for firewood, food, and building materials. That dependence cuts both ways. Wood fuel accounts for a large share of household energy use across the Miombo region, which keeps pressure on the woodland high even where restoration work is underway. Providing communities with alternative income sources, rather than relying solely on wood and charcoal, is central to keeping any restored area intact over the long term. Alongside the restoration targets, the project will establish three plant nurseries to supply seedlings for ongoing work. Planners also intend to develop beekeeping and support sustainable value chains tied to cashew, bamboo, and legally harvested timber. Those activities aim to give residents income tied directly to keeping the landscape intact, a key piece of how forest landscape restoration in Mozambique is meant to work in practice. Forest landscape restoration in Mozambique ties livelihood directly to conservation, with three community nurseries, beekeeping, and sustainable value chains for cashew, bamboo, and timber giving Nampula residents concrete economic reasons to keep the landscape intact. Photo courtesy of IUCN . Mozambique’s project forms part of a larger global effort known as the FLR Hub, implemented by IUCN alongside other international partners. The hub originally supported restoration work across six countries in Africa and Latin America. A new contribution from Switzerland, announced in late 2025, extended that reach to Mozambique, bringing the total to seven participating countries. According to IUCN, the hub aims to shift restoration efforts from scattered, one-off projects to coordinated approaches that attract long-term investment. That shift matters for a landscape as large and fragmented as the Miombo, where piecemeal efforts have struggled to keep pace with ongoing degradation. Implementation in Ribáuè will rely on continued collaboration between government agencies, private businesses, universities, and civil society groups. Success will depend on whether restored land can deliver real income for residents, not just healthier soil and more trees. Four years is a short window to prove that the model works, but it gives the project a clear point at which results can be measured against the hectare targets set at launch. If it works, forest landscape restoration in Mozambique could offer a model other Miombo countries draw on as they pursue their own restoration commitments. The post Forest Landscape Restoration in Mozambique Launches in Nampula Province appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: The next time you pick up a notebook, pause for a moment. An earthy brown cover , a leaf logo, or the words 'eco-friendly' might make it look like the greener choice. But appearances can be deceptive. What you should consider is the paper inside, the materials used to make it, how long it lasts, and whether it can be recycled after use. For Ashutosh Ananth, co-founder of paper and stationery brand 'Rescript' , sustainability is about looking beyond appearances and rethinking how everyday paper products are made. "A notebook being sustainable is about much more than having a kraft cover or looking natural. You have to look at what it is made from, how it is put together, how long it will last, and what happens to it after you are done using it," he says. Founded in 2021 by Ashutosh and his school friend Naren Raj, the brand makes copier paper, notebooks, journals, planners, and other stationery using 100 percent recycled paper. After pursuing ideas such as biofuels in 2019, the friends entered corporate gifting. That experience showed them how much paper businesses consume every day. "We realised that the opportunity was much larger than gifting. If we could make everyday paper products more sustainable, the impact could be greater," he says. Recycled paper and notebooks became their starting point, eventually growing into a wider stationery range. So, what should you look for when buying a notebook? The co-founder shares six things consumers should check before making a choice. 1. Check what the paper is made from Since paper makes up most of a notebook, its composition is the first thing to examine. Rather than relying on broad descriptions such as 'eco-friendly', 'green' or 'sustainable', he recommends looking for a clear statement of the recycled content. Founded in 2021 by Ashutosh and his school friend Naren Raj, the brand makes copier paper, notebooks, journals, planners, and other stationery using 100 percent recycled paper. "A notebook made with 100 percent recycled paper reduces the need for virgin fibre and gives already-used paper another life," he explains. The percentage matters. A notebook containing 10 or 20 percent recycled fibre is different from one made entirely from recycled paper, even though both may be marketed as containing recycled material. If virgin fibre is used, consumers should also look for information about whether it is responsibly sourced. "Look at the fibre composition, including how much is recycled and where any virgin fibre comes from," he adds. 2. Look for credible certifications Claims are more meaningful when independently verified. Ashutosh recommends checking recognised labels such as the Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) and the Programme for the Endorsement of Forest Certification (PEFC), while understanding what each means. An FSC Recycled label verifies that the relevant fibre is 100 percent recycled. FSC Mix, on the other hand, can include a combination of recycled material, FSC-certified virgin fibre and controlled virgin fibre. "A precisely stated fibre composition, certification number, and manufacturing information tell you much more than a brown cover with a leaf printed on it," he says. 3. Do not judge the paper by its colour Brown, beige, and grey paper are mostly associated with sustainability. But a notebook's colour alone cannot tell you how responsibly it has been made. "A brownish or grey notebook does not necessarily mean it is more sustainable," he says. "Colour can tell you something about how the paper has been processed, but it does not tell you enough about where the fibre came from, how much of it is recycled, or how responsibly the notebook has been made." Bright white paper may undergo additional processing, bleaching, and optical brightening. Recycled paper can also be made bright white, while virgin paper can be brown or beige. "Rescript uses careful sourcing, segregation, de-inking, and controlled processing, while avoiding chlorine bleaching, to achieve its natural warm-white shade. For us, the goal was never just to make recycled paper. It was to make recycled paper that people would choose because it is good paper," he explains. 4. Examine the cover and finishing A notebook may contain recycled paper but still include materials that make it harder to recycle. Plastic lamination, synthetic covers, heavy coatings, foil, and other decorative finishes can add to the number of materials used. When these are permanently bonded to paper, separating them at the end of the notebook's life can become more difficult. Recycled paper and notebooks became their starting point, eventually growing into a wider stationery range. "It is common to talk about sustainable paper while adding heavily laminated, plastic-coated or synthetic covers around it," he says. He recommends paper-based or recycled covers and avoiding finishes that serve little practical purpose. 5. Make sure it is built to last Sustainability is not only about what a notebook is made from. It is also about how long it remains useful. A notebook with weak pages, poor binding, or a cover that falls apart prematurely may need to be replaced before it has served its purpose. "A notebook that falls apart halfway through its life and has to be replaced is not particularly sustainable," the co-founder says. Check the binding, paper strength, and construction. Thread binding keeps materials relatively simple, while a metal spiral can usually be separated from the paper before recycling. "Choosing to stay sustainable should not mean accepting an inferior product," he says. "The ideal is to get both things right. A lower-impact material and a genuinely good product made from it." 6. Consider what happens after the last page Ashutosh recommends choosing products with easier construction and fewer unnecessary non-paper components. Once a notebook has been completely used, removable metal spirals and other separable parts should be taken off where possible. Plastic lamination, glitter, foil, and heavy coatings deserve particular attention because some can interfere with the recovery of paper fibres. Recyclability also depends on the facilities available locally, so consumers should check what their local recycler accepts. "The less the construction, the easier it generally is to recover and recycle the materials," he says. His advice is to use the notebook fully, separate removable components, keep the paper clean and dry, and check local guidance. "Recyclability is not just about whether a material can theoretically be recycled somewhere in the world. It is about whether the product has been designed sensibly enough, and whether the recycling system available to you can actually recover it," he explains. Turning recycled paper into an everyday choice For Ashutosh and Naren, these considerations are central to Rescript's effort to make recycled paper a common choice for consumers and businesses. Their paper is made from 100 percent recycled material and processed without chlorine bleaching. Its published comparisons state that the paper uses around 50 percent less water and produces 37 percent lower carbon dioxide emissions than its conventional paper benchmark. The company holds FSC certification under licence code FSC C163185. Since paper makes up most of a notebook, its composition is the first thing to examine. As of September 2026, it has used more than 1,000 tonnes of recycled paper since its launch. The company estimates that this represents more than 18,000 trees saved, around four crore litres of water conserved and approximately 13 lakh kilograms of carbon dioxide emissions avoided compared with producing an equivalent quantity through conventional virgin-paper processes. It now supplies products to individual customers as well as institutional and corporate buyers, including DMart, JP Morgan, Hero MotoCorp, LIC, and ICICI Prudential. Ashutosh says replacing conventional paper at scale can accelerate the impact. "We use recycled paper because we believe it is the right material choice, but the ambition is not only to make a sustainable notebook. It is to make a notebook that someone would choose for its paper, texture, construction, and experience even if sustainability were not the first thing on their mind," he concludes. All pictures courtesy Rescript.

Η θεραπεία, που ονομάζεται Μαγνητική e-Resonance Therapy (MeRT), αναπτύχθηκε από την Wave Neuroscience με έδρα την Καλιφόρνια σε συνεργασία με…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A newly FDA-cleared treatment for PTSD reported 68 percent remission in clinical trials. The best-performing approved medications for the condition top out at around 10.9 percent. The treatment, called Magnetic e-Resonance Therapy (MeRT), was developed by California-based Wave Neuroscience in collaboration with researchers at the Texas A&M Health Institute of Biosciences and Technology. It pairs brain activity mapping with personalized magnetic stimulation. The clinical trial also reported a 52 percent reduction in PTSD symptoms overall. “Our FDA trial reported a 52 percent reduction in symptoms, so more than a four-fold increase in efficacy,” said Erik Won, D.O., Wave Neuroscience’s chief medical officer. “And more importantly, we saw 68 percent remission in our clinical trial. From a clinical care perspective, that’s really meaningful.” These results come from different studies, not a direct head-to-head comparison, but the gap is hard to ignore. How MeRT personalizes treatment The process starts with an electroencephalogram (EEG) that records each patient’s brain electrical activity. An AI-assisted algorithm uses that data to build a personalized stimulation plan. A coil placed against the scalp then delivers targeted magnetic pulses through transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), a technique already FDA-cleared for treatment-resistant depression . Standard TMS follows a generalized protocol. MeRT adjusts based on what’s happening in each patient’s brain. Dr. Kenneth S. Ramos, a precision medicine researcher at Texas A&M Health who helped guide the study, put it this way: standard TMS covers the leak with a tarp; MeRT tries to find and replace the damaged shingles. Participants received five sessions per week over five to six weeks, but improvements appeared to persist after the sessions ended. The first FDA-cleared non-drug option for PTSD PTSD was formally recognized as a diagnosis in 1980 . Since then, treatment has relied on two FDA-approved medications, both SSRIs, and psychotherapy. A 2020 review found medication remission rates reached 10.9 percent at most. MeRT will be the first FDA-cleared non-medication treatment specifically for PTSD. Dr. Israel Liberzon, the study’s lead psychiatrist and a distinguished professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at the Texas A&M Naresh K. Vashisht College of Medicine, explained what that means for patients. “Right now, the FDA has approved only two medications for PTSD,” he said. “This is the first time that in addition to the medication, we have a non-medication option. There is psychotherapy that people use for PTSD, but psychotherapies require a lot of effort. People must participate actively, and many drop out because it’s too anxiety-provoking. So now we have a unique alternative.” About six percent of Americans will experience PTSD during their lifetime, with higher rates among women and veterans . In the United States, approximately 17.5 veterans die by suicide each day. “People living with PTSD have been left with trial-and-error treatment, medications and their side effects, and limited outcomes—even when treated by the most dedicated and experienced physicians,” Won said. “Wave’s FDA clearance signals a fundamentally different future: one in which PTSD can be objectively evaluated, precisely treated and meaningfully healed.” Wave Neuroscience and Texas A&M Health are working on insurance coverage to make the therapy more widely accessible. Won also believes MeRT could eventually be adapted for depression, anxiety, and other psychiatric conditions. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post Personalized brain therapy hits 68 percent remission for PTSD first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Chances are, you’ve got a tube of toothpaste in your bathroom right now. If it’s only going on your teeth, you’re leaving a surprisingly useful cleaning tool sitting on your bathroom counter. Joy Ramos , a professional cleaner and operations manager at Bear Bros Cleaning, has long used toothpaste for jobs well beyond the bathroom. Most white, non-gel toothpastes contain mild abrasive particles that work like ultra-fine sandpaper, polishing surfaces without scratching them. It turns out that property has a lot of household uses. One thing before you start: plain white, non-gel toothpaste is what you want. Gel formulas don’t have the same abrasive particles, and heavily whitening varieties can be too harsh on delicate surfaces. Always rinse thoroughly after using it, and when in doubt, test on a discreet spot first. For scratches and cloudy surfaces A light scratch on glass (a phone screen, a coffee table, a mirror) can often be buffed out with a small amount of toothpaste on a microfiber cloth. Work in gentle circles, then wipe clean. The abrasives smooth the area around the scratch rather than filling it, so it becomes much less visible. The same trick works on fogged car headlights. Rub toothpaste over the lens in small circular motions for a minute or two, then rinse and dry. Repeat if needed. Wood is another one. Water rings and minor scratches on countertops or floors respond well to a small amount applied with a soft cloth. Follow the grain, wipe off, and dry thoroughly. For metals and fixtures Hard water takes the shine out of faucets and handles over time. Toothpaste can bring it back on stainless steel and chrome, though there’s a catch: softer metals like copper and brass can be damaged by the abrasives, so skip those. Silver jewelry is a great candidate, too. Avoid polished metals and soft stones like opals, pearls, or turquoise. “Always use a gentle hand and test first,” Ramos says. For walls, shoes, and more Crayon on painted walls is a classic small-kid problem. Toothpaste can lift it, but the wall finish matters. “Due to the mild abrasives in the paste, flat or matte paint may sometimes fade or become damaged,” Ramos says. “And on darker or more delicate finishes, it could leave dull spots or streaks.” Glossy, light-colored paint holds up well. Toothpaste also works on white rubber soles and leather or canvas sneakers. Just keep it away from suede, mesh, or anything delicate; those materials can stain or break down. For a persistent stain on a toilet seat, apply a small amount with a cloth or toothbrush, scrub gently, let it sit a few minutes, and wipe clean. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: “Vibe coding,” is so last year. If you want to (try) to get on the same wavelength as teens and tweens, here’s another expression to add to your repertoire: Collins Dictionary has selected “mogging” as its 2026 word of the year. The slang term popular among Gen Z and Gen Alpha is defined as outperforming or outshining someone or something. Believed to be a shortened version of AMOG (alpha male of the group), the word traces back to bodybuilding culture around the 2010s. But it’s soared in popularity over the past year, with younger generations using it in a more playful way. Collins noted that experts found a 210% increase in usage of the “fast-growing slang word” in 2026, meriting the “word of the year” crown. So how do you use it? If your friend looks amazing in the selfie you just took, but your eyes are closed and hair is out of place — they’re mogging you. Or, to offer a more meta example, mogging is mogging the other words in the dictionary. Other words on the British dictionary’s shortlist include: Bixie : a haircut that’s shorter than a bob but longer than a pixie cut Fricy : a blend of fruity and spicy Friendslop : a low-budget, independently made video game designed to be played casually with friends Carspreading : the tendency of manufacturers to build cars that are longer, wider, and heavier Hydration break : a pause in a sporting contest to allow the contestants to drink fluids, especially in high heat Ghost job : a role advertised by an employer who has no intention of actually hiring anyone On Oct. 25, Dictionary.com announced its own word of the year: “Maxxing,” a shortened version of “maximizing” that can be used on its own or tacked on to the end of another word to describe the act of optimizing something. Derived from gamer lingo and in use for over a decade, the slang term broke through on TikTok in the 2020s. Its most famous usage is perhaps “looksmaxxing,” which refers to taking a person’s appearance to its full potential, but “sleepmaxxing,” “cozymaxxing,” and “booksmaxxing” have all joined the zeitgeist as well. “Really, anything in your life can get the maxxing treatment, if you do it wholeheartedly enough,” the online dictionary wrote in a blog post.

items.descriptionOriginal: P undits are describing last night as a romp for Democrats, a rebuke of Republicans, a blue tsunami, a rout in the red states. But underneath these headlines is a quieter, parallel story about voters choosing to abandon tribal allegiance and make decisions for themselves. For months, we’ve been hearing about the possibility of a blue wave — and then, in the same breath, the caveat: Is a wave even possible in today’s hyper-polarized America? And yet, in Texas, Florida, Kansas and beyond, the electorate refused to let party loyalty make their choice for them. Young, Latino and red-state voters moved, sometimes dramatically, in just two years. The composition of the two sides turned out to be less fixed than we imagined, with a meaningful number of voters willing to cast ballots across party lines when a candidate, issue or circumstance spoke to them. In Texas, where Democrats had historic wins, people of all parties have recently united to fight against a border wall through Big Bend National Park. Credit: Sam Karas Part of the story was turnout, said New York Times Chief Political Analyst Nate Cohn on The Daily . But, he added, “Many people who are registered as Republicans and voted for Donald Trump voted for the Democratic candidate.” This feels like a fitting conclusion to The Depolarization Project , our special series about how political polarization works and what we can do about it. The premise of that series was that depolarization isn’t about meeting in the middle. It’s about choosing to remain open and curious, rather than blindly clinging to arbitrary affiliations. In the end, many voters showed that their party label doesn’t have the final say. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The Walkable Traveler: Discovering Philadelphia’s Greenest Neighborhoods on Foot Reading Time: 3 minutes The Walkable Traveler: Discovering Philadelphia’s Greenest Neighborhoods on Foot There’s a moment on most city breaks when you realise you’ve spent more time getting between places than actually enjoying them. You’ve waited for a taxi, sat in traffic, arrived somewhere only to discover it’s a ten-minute walk from where you were half an hour ago. It’s enough to make you wonder why you bothered with the car in the first place. Philadelphia is a city where I’d be inclined to leave it behind.Not everywhere is within walking distance, obviously, but a surprising amount of the central area is. The streets are laid out in a fairly straightforward grid, and there’s plenty to see without travelling particularly far. I’d probably start somewhere around Independence Hall, partly because it’s one of those places you feel you ought to visit, and partly because the surrounding streets are worth a look in their own right. From there, Reading Terminal Market isn’t too far away. I wouldn’t bother making elaborate lunch plans. With that many food stalls under one roof, you’re almost certain to find something you fancy, although deciding what to eat might take longer than expected. Afterward, you could head towards Rittenhouse Square. I rather like the idea of a park that doesn’t try too hard to be an attraction. Rittenhouse is simply a pleasant place to sit for a while, with trees, benches and people going about their day. Somebody’s reading a book. Somebody else is walking a dog that clearly has no intention of going home yet. Meanwhile, the surrounding streets are full of shops, restaurants and apartments. It feels like a proper part of the neighbourhood rather than somewhere created exclusively for visitors. Philadelphia has quite a few green spaces like that, although some are much smaller. Community gardens are particularly interesting. You might find one occupying what was once an empty lot, with vegetables growing in raised beds and a few chairs tucked into a corner. They aren’t necessarily places you’d travel across the city to visit. But coming across one while walking through a residential neighbourhood is rather lovely. And they tell you something about the people who live there. I’d also make time for South Philadelphia. East Passyunk Avenue has the sort of mixture I enjoy: independent shops, restaurants, cafés and ordinary residential streets just around the corner. You can wander without feeling you’re missing some major attraction because you haven’t followed a particular route. The nearby Italian Market area is worth including too, especially if you like looking around food shops. I’d probably end up buying something completely impractical to carry around for the rest of the afternoon. One thing I wouldn’t do is try to squeeze all of Philadelphia into a single walking itinerary. It’s a sizeable city, and there’s no prize for finishing your holiday with sore feet. SEPTA’s buses, trolleys and trains make it possible to cover longer distances without needing a car, which is useful if you want to explore beyond the central neighbourhoods. Where you stay can make the whole thing easier or considerably more annoying. I once heard somebody describe a hotel as being ‘only twenty minutes from everything’, which sounds wonderful until you realise they meant twenty minutes by car. For a trip focused on walking, I’d be looking at the actual streets around the accommodation. Is there somewhere nearby for breakfast? Can you reach a park without crossing several major roads? How far is the nearest transit stop? Those details matter more to me than whether the apartment has an especially impressive television. One of the most effective ways to practice eco-friendly travel is reducing reliance on automobiles during city visits. Philadelphia’s grid layout makes it one of the most pedestrian- and transit-friendly cities in North America, allowing visitors to walk from historic landmarks to local farmers’ markets with ease. Choosing a neighborhood rental situated near public transportation hubs and neighborhood parks allows travelers to experience authentic community life while keeping emissions low. Rather than juggling multiple booking platforms, smart travelers use independent meta-search portals to find well-located accommodations. Exploring Philadelphia vacation rentals via cozycozy gives travelers real-time access to available townhomes, lofts, and historic suites across every major rental portal, making it effortless to lock in a sustainable home base. I’d check the final booking details separately, particularly the exact location and any additional charges. Of course, there’s an environmental benefit to doing more of a city break on foot. Fewer car journeys generally mean fewer transport emissions , and using public transport for longer trips can help reduce your reliance on taxis or a hire car. But I wouldn’t spend the whole weekend thinking about my carbon footprint.I’d be thinking about where to get another coffee, whether there’s time to explore one more street and why I hadn’t left myself longer at the market. That’s probably what makes walking such a good way to experience Philadelphia. You get to see the famous buildings, but you also spend time in the places between them. The little gardens, the corner shops, the streets where nothing especially remarkable is happening.And sometimes those are the bits you remember most.
