items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Goldman Prize Honors Young Activist for Stopping Fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River Towns Reading Time: 3 minutes Yuvelis Morales Blanco won the 2026 Goldman Environmental Prize for stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River communities and helping halt two pilot projects and secure a landmark court ruling. A university student began stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River towns by knocking on her neighbors’ doors. Seven years later, Yuvelis Morales Blanco has won the 2026 Goldman Environmental Prize for that work. The prize honors grassroots environmental leaders from six world regions each year. Her campaign helped stop two pilot fracking projects near her hometown of Puerto Wilches. It also led to a Constitutional Court ruling that upheld her Afro-Colombian community’s right to a say. To date, no fracking project has moved forward anywhere in Colombia. Morales Blanco, now 24, grew up in a family of subsistence fishers on the Magdalena River. The river flows nearly 1,000 miles from the Andes to the Caribbean, about the distance from Boston to Atlanta. For the roughly 30,000 people of Puerto Wilches, it provides food, income, and identity. The town also sits in the heart of Colombia’s oil country. Ecopetrol, the largest and majority state-owned oil company, is based in nearby Barrancabermeja. Between 2015 and 2022, about 40% of its more than 2,000 oil spills happened in this region. That works out to roughly two spills a week for eight years. In 2018, a leak at the Lizama 158 well displaced about 100 families and killed thousands of fish. So when the government proposed fracking nearby, residents had reason to worry. In 2019, then-President Iván Duque announced two pilot projects called Kalé and Platero. Ecopetrol led both, with ExxonMobil as operator and majority partner on Platero. Fracking, short for hydraulic fracturing, pumps water, sand, and chemicals into rock at high pressure. The pressure cracks the rock and frees trapped oil or gas. The process uses large amounts of water and can contaminate rivers and groundwater. Morales Blanco was studying environmental engineering at the time. She paused her degree and began visiting neighbors to explain the risks. She also joined the Alianza Colombia Libre de Fracking, or Colombia Free from Fracking Alliance. With the alliance, she helped lead protests outside the Ecopetrol refinery. In January 2022, she testified at permit hearings and organized a peaceful sit-in. Soon after the sit-in, armed men showed up at her home. She fled Colombia, and France granted her asylum in February 2022. No one has been convicted for the threats against her. Exile in France did not end her campaign. She received the Marianne Initiative award for human rights defenders and raised the issue with President Emmanuel Macron. She also brought the case before the International Rights of Nature Tribunal. Back home, the campaign for stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River towns began winning in court. In April 2022, a court suspended environmental permits for both projects until companies consulted local communities. Months later, newly elected President Gustavo Petro announced his opposition to fracking. Community organizing helped secure a court-ordered suspension of two fracking projects in 2022, a key step in stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River, followed months later by President Gustavo Petro’s opposition to fracking. Photo by Christian Escobar Mora courtesy of Goldman Environmental Prize . Ecopetrol suspended the project contracts in September 2022. By November, it had halted Kalé and Platero and undone its agreements with ExxonMobil. The decisive ruling came in August 2024. Colombia’s Constitutional Court found that the pilots violated the community’s right to free, prior, and informed consent. Under this principle, companies must consult communities and win their agreement before projects affect their land. That decision reaches beyond Puerto Wilches. It confirms that Afro-Colombian communities have a legal voice over what happens on their territory. The precedent matters for stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River communities and anywhere similar projects appear. Morales Blanco has since returned to Puerto Wilches and keeps organizing with the alliance. She describes the Magdalena as the life that sustains her family and her fishing community. She also points out that her region produces great energy wealth while many residents stay poor. The Global Greengrants Fund, which supports the alliance, notes that each prize winner represents a broader movement. More than 80 of the fund’s partners and allies have received the prize since 1993. Afro-Colombian fishing communities stood beside her in stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River towns. Morales Blanco won for the South and Central America region, one of six 2026 winners , all of whom were women. The others came from Nigeria, South Korea, the United Kingdom, Papua New Guinea, and the United States. Colombia’s politics have shifted since her win. President Abelardo de la Espriella took office in August 2026 after campaigning to expand fracking. Still, the 2024 ruling gives communities like Puerto Wilches firm legal ground to demand a say. Stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River communities didn’t require a big budget or political office. It took a young woman who knew her river and kept going after threats forced her abroad. Her prize shows how local action can shape national policy. The post Goldman Prize Honors Young Activist for Stopping Fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River Towns appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.title: Τετράγωνα αγάπης που ηρεμούσαν ένα παιδί
items.titleOriginal: Squares of Love that Calmed a Child
items.description: Ένα μικρό πλεκτό σωληνάκι —ανοιχτό και στις δύο άκρες, αρκετά φαρδύ για δύο χέρια — και ένα παιδί με άγχος βρέθηκαν σε μια αυστριακή τάξη. Αυτή η ήσυχη στιγμή βρίσκεται στο επίκεντρο του δεκαετούς έργου της Ursula Kermer, Mehr ist Mehr ("More is More"), ένα δίκτυο εθελοντών που μετατρέπει μεμονωμένα τετράγωνα νήματος σε κουβέρτες, μπολερό και κουβέρτες.…
items.descriptionOriginal: A small knitted tube — open at both ends, just wide enough for two hands — and a child with anxiety found each other in an Austrian classroom. That quiet moment is at the heart of Ursula Kermer's decade-long project, Mehr ist Mehr ("More is More"), a volunteer network that turns individual squares of yarn into blankets, boleros, and twiddle muffs for people moving through hard seasons of life. Kermer, an art therapist, is honest about what the project cannot do: "Our project does not solve problems; it does not make crisis go away." But it is constant, and that constancy — the weekly knitting circles, the puzzling together of mismatched squares, the packages of wool arriving unbidden from strangers — turns out to be its own kind of medicine. The blankets travel to families whose children have cancer, to people who cannot pay their heating bills, to rehabilitation centers where a counselor leaves them draped over chairs so that someone in crisis might simply reach out and choose one. Most knitters never know whose hands will eventually hold their work, and Kermer photographs every step so they know where it ends — just not with whom. She describes the whole endeavor as resilience training in disguise: choosing a color, trusting a process, watching mismatched pieces become something whole. For her, the image that holds it all is a network — "growing and moving, and provides a resilient safety" — as easily overlooked, but just as strong as the individual threads that compose spools of yarn.

items.description: Happy Eco News Οι Cofán Rangers προστατεύουν τη φρουρά του Αμαζονίου 450.000 εκτάρια τροπικού δάσους του Ισημερινού Χρόνος ανάγνωσης: 3 λεπτά Οι δασοφύλακες της Cofán που προστατεύουν τον Αμαζόνιο μεταφέρουν δέματα 100 λιβρών σε περιπολίες διάρκειας μηνών, υπερασπίζοντας την περιοχή των προγονικών τροπικών δασών που ωφελεί ολόκληρο τον πλανήτη. Οι δασοφύλακες της Cofán που προστατεύουν τον Αμαζόνιο έχουν διαφυλάξει τον Εκουαδόρ…
items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Cofán Rangers Protecting the Amazon Guard 450,000 Hectares of Ecuadorian Rainforest Reading Time: 3 minutes Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon carry 100-pound packs on monthlong patrols, defending ancestral rainforest territory that benefits the entire planet. The Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon have safeguarded the Ecuadorian rainforest for centuries, living where the Amazon Basin rises toward the Andes. Among the region’s oldest surviving indigenous cultures, the Cofán now protect more than one million acres of ancestral territory, roughly the size of the U.S. state of Delaware, containing primary forest, wild rivers, swamplands, and several thousand plant and animal species found nowhere else. That protection intensified after oil exploitation and the colonists who followed threatened to overwhelm Cofán lands. In response, Cofán leadership founded Fundación Sobrevivencia Cofán in 1999, an organization built on what its founders described as a fight-for-rights-or-disappear mindset. The Cofán Survival Fund, an independent U.S.-based nonprofit, supports that work by channeling donations directly into Cofán-led conservation programs. At the center of Cofán people’s protection of the Amazon is GuardAmazonas Cofán, formerly known as the Cofán Park Guards. Since 2003, teams of Cofán rangers have delimited, secured, monitored, and protected their homeland, using GPS units and drones to gather intelligence on threats before coordinating with police and the military to counter illegal incursions. The program’s success convinced Ecuador’s Ministry of Environment to more than double the Cofán’s legally recognized ancestral territory. Today, nearly 50 Cofán rangers patrol in five-person teams, carrying full packs on monthlong expeditions that demand extreme physical fitness and deep forest knowledge. Unlike many indigenous territory-protection programs, GuardAmazonas pays its rangers, recognizing that sustained, full-time conservation work demands fair compensation for families bearing real costs and risks. Teams deliberately mix members from different communities and generations, transmitting ecological knowledge across the Cofán homeland while strengthening unified national identity. Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon through GuardAmazonas receive fair pay for sustained, full-time conservation work, with patrol teams deliberately mixing members from different communities and generations to transmit ecological knowledge across the Cofán homeland. Photo courtesy of Cofán Survival Fund . The work of Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon extends well beyond ranger patrols into cultural survival and scientific partnership. Between 2001 and 2008, the foundation coordinated four Rapid Biological Inventories with Chicago Field Museum biologists, leading directly to expanded territorial protection. That collaboration earned a 2013 MacArthur Award for Creative and Effective Institutions. The Charapa Project shows how Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon lead species recovery. Commercial egg harvesting nearly eliminated the Amazonian river turtle from Ecuadorian beaches until Cofán communities began raising hatchlings in protected ponds in the 1980s, dramatically improving survival rates before release. In Zábalo, families now protect most turtle nests they find, and travelers along the Aguarico River encounter river turtles sunning themselves on nearly every log once they enter Cofán territory, a result confirmed by peer-reviewed research co-authored by Cofán community members. Climate change has not spared Cofán lands, prompting the creation of the Lifeboat Garden Project. As scorching temperatures and unpredictable rainfall diminished important food and medicinal plant species, project leaders transplanted them to more ecologically stable upriver land, preserving botanical knowledge for future generations while protecting additional forest in a heavily deforested area. Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon also invest in human capital. The Cofán Higher Education Project sends entire families, not just individual students, to Quito, where parents pursue university degrees while children attend quality schools, preserving language and cultural identity through shared communal housing. The Seguro Campesino Project enrolls Cofán families in Ecuadorian social welfare programs, sends medical brigades to remote communities, and removes financial pressures that might otherwise force compromises on territorial conservation commitments. Innovation among Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon also extends to transportation. After the successful Ecocanoa Project taught Cofán artisans to build durable fiberglass canoes instead of felling endangered trees, the Solar Canoe Project now develops battery-powered alternatives to fossil-fuel motors, creating quieter waterways that benefit wildlife, hunting, fishing, and ecotourism alike. Ecotourism remains central to Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon, tracing back to the 1970s, when FSC founder Randy Borman and Cofán community members began hosting visitors along the Aguarico River and eventually established the community of Zábalo. Rather than staging performances, Cofán guides position themselves as credentialed experts who share ecological knowledge directly, keeping more revenue by controlling ecotourism operations rather than losing profits to outside intermediaries. Felipe Borman, current Executive Director of the foundation and recently elected Director of Territory for the Cofán ethnic federation NOA’IKE, continues work his father Randy began, coordinating fieldwork across the Cofán-Bermejo Ecological Reserve and Río Cofanes Territory. The foundation’s Rapid Response Team stays vigilant over changing laws and policies that threaten Cofán land rights, while accompanying patients through Ecuador’s healthcare system and coordinating visits from scientists, officials, and allies. As climate negotiations worldwide increasingly recognize indigenous stewardship as essential to global conservation outcomes, Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon demonstrate what sustained, community-led territorial defense can achieve. The foundation emphasizes that funding Cofán rangers protects the forest the whole world depends on, not just Cofán communities, positioning indigenous-led conservation as climate infrastructure that benefits everyone far beyond Ecuador’s Amazonian lowlands. items.description: Αυτό το άρθρο γράφτηκε από τη Stephanie Szarmach, μεταδιδακτορικό συνεργάτη James Smithson στο Smithsonian Institution, για το The Conversation — έναν μη κερδοσκοπικό ειδησεογραφικό οργανισμό αφιερωμένο στην ανταλλαγή γνώσεων ερευνητών και επιστημόνων, με άδεια Creative Commons. Διαβάστε το πρωτότυπο άρθρο εδώ. Στραβίζοντας μέσα από τα κιάλια μου, σάρωση th…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Stephanie Szarmach , a James Smithson Postdoctoral Fellow at the Smithsonian Institution, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . Squinting through my binoculars, I scanned the dense branches of a black spruce, trying my best to catch a glimpse of the thin legs of a small black, white, and yellow songbird. I was on the hunt for a yellow-rumped warbler — a bird affectionately called “butter-butt” by bird-watchers after the distinctive buttery yellow patch of feathers above its tail. Once I spotted a flash of red on one of the bird’s legs, I knew that this individual was special — in fact, it was one that I already knew well. That’s because I had placed identifying bands on it the previous year as part of my Ph.D. research , and it was carrying a very important piece of new technology. Johanna Beam Stephanie Szarmach holds a yellow-rumped warbler that was banded as part of a study. I played the high-pitched “warble ” of its song through a speaker placed below a mist net of fine, nearly invisible mesh. Thinking another male had intruded on his territory, the bird quickly descended. My tactic worked — he got caught in the net. As I gently removed him, I breathed a sigh of relief as I saw the Tic Tac-size device sitting on his back. Over the past year, this warbler carried a multisensor geolocator backpack throughout his migratory journey, recording the long trek from his breeding grounds in Anchorage, Alaska, to a yet unknown winter refuge and back again. Working with my Ph.D. adviser, evolutionary biologist David Toews , I deployed dozens of these cutting-edge tags to illuminate the migratory journeys of these high-latitude breeding warblers at a scale not previously possible for small birds. Stephanie Szarmach A yellow-rumped warbler wears a multisensor geolocator backpack. Now, after a year of waiting, I finally had the data in hand. How Can Scientists Track Small Birds? Researchers began tracking the movements of migrating birds in the late 1960s using radio telemetry , a technique that requires tagged birds to be physically followed with receiver equipment, sometimes aided by a small aircraft. Then, as GPS became more widely available in the early 2000s, satellite tags let researchers accurately track birds remotely. However, GPS transmitters are hefty — even just the battery that powers them is too heavy to be carried by the majority of small migratory songbirds, which often weigh less than a spoonful of sugar. To address this problem, researchers developed ingenious little light-level geolocators . These miniature tags minimize weight by containing only a tiny battery, clock, computer chip, and light sensor. They store data internally rather than transmitting it — hence my need to recapture tagged birds a year later. Researchers infer a bird’s locations from the timing of sunrise and sunset, which vary predictably across the globe and throughout the year. Stephanie Szarmach Each harness loop of the multisensor geolocator goes around one of the bird’s legs and the tag sits on the bird’s lower back. Light-level geolocators have opened new windows into the migrations of small birds , but they also have limitations: Their estimated locations can err by hundreds of miles, and this uncertainty becomes impractically high around the equinoxes, when day length is the same worldwide. More recently, researchers developed a newer method of geolocation that uses atmospheric pressure to circumvent these limitations. When a bird ascends during a migratory flight, a barometric geolocator records a steep drop in air pressure, capturing the timing of departure and arrival for every stop along a bird’s migration route. In between flights, the pressure the tag records reflects the elevation at the bird’s position. Knowing the bird’s elevation helps to narrow down possible locations, which researchers can then refine further by comparing the change in pressure over time recorded by the tag to global weather data using the computer program GeoPressureR . The unique pattern of rises and falls in pressure acts as a kind of pressure fingerprint for a specific location. Including light and wind data in the model of the bird’s movements can increase precision even more. Stephanie Szarmach Atmospheric pressure data collected from a multisensor geolocator carried by a yellow-rumped warbler over five days in spring. When the bird is stationary, such as when resting at a stopover site, the measured pressure remains steady. During migratory flights, when the bird ascends into the sky, the pressure drops and fluctuates dramatically. New Tech Answers an Old Question We used these new multisensor backpacks to study the migration patterns of myrtle warblers , the northern subspecies of yellow-rumped warbler, which breed across North America’s boreal forest. Myrtle warblers in the northeast are known to winter along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts, but where northwestern populations migrate has been more of a mystery. In 1899, ornithologist Richard McGregor observed myrtle warblers wintering in coastal California , and hypothesized that these birds might breed in Alaska and British Columbia. Using these new tags allowed us to test whether warblers breeding in Anchorage, Alaska, actually followed the shortest migration route to winter in California. To our surprise — and probably to McGregor’s as well, if he were still alive — we found that all the birds we tracked traveled east across the boreal forest of Canada before shifting south to the Gulf Coast – certainly not the Pacific Coast route we expected. All told, this 6,800-mile (10,900-kilometer) round-trip journey was much longer than we anticipated for a species commonly considered a short- or medium-distance migrant. Figure by Stephanie Szarmach. Warbler illustration by Emily Griffith Researchers tracked the routes six myrtle warblers flew on their fall migration southeast from Anchorage, Alaska. Why Take Such a Circuitous Route? The long, seemingly suboptimal route taken by our Alaskan myrtle warblers is actually mirrored by some other songbird species tracked from northwestern North America, including blackpoll warblers and Swainson’s thrushes . Part of this pattern may relate back to the glaciations that isolated ancient populations of birds millions of years ago. The thinking goes that as these glaciers spread, they squashed the ranges of formerly northern species into the south. Then, as the glaciers slowly receded, the forests gradually reexpanded. As more land opened up, birds moved farther north and west into that habitat. Each season some birds went a little farther as the forest available in their northern breeding grounds expanded. For migratory species such as myrtle warblers, the farther north and west their breeding range expanded, the longer the migration to their southern wintering ground became. Scientists think migration routes are genetically encoded . The birds’ genes may have traced this expansion front, like Hansel and Gretel putting down breadcrumbs as they journeyed deeper and deeper into the forest. Today’s migration routes still trace that incrementally expanded path, even though the glaciers that shaped the original boundaries are long gone. We’re still not sure exactly where the California-wintering myrtle warblers spotted in the 1800s are breeding. We suspect that a small proportion of the Anchorage-breeding birds may migrate to California , but that most of them travel from more distant, unstudied regions of Alaska or Yukon. Future research, potentially tagging myrtle warblers directly on the California wintering grounds, will shed more light on this population and why certain individuals follow a different migration route. Barometric Geolocation Provides New Data Today, this new geolocation approach improves scientists’ ability to study the migrations of small birds and supports more effective conservation actions across the course of the entire year . More precise location estimates help researchers identify key stopover and wintering sites in need of protection and better understand the threats birds face throughout their journeys. These geolocators also reveal the altitude of migratory flights, which is important for understanding the risk of birds colliding with buildings or wind turbines. Because these new tags capture pressure data for every migratory flight, they’re especially valuable for studying migration timing. Researchers have combined data from over 50 bird species to understand at what time of day or night different birds migrate . Now, as a postdoctoral researcher at the Smithsonian Migratory Bird Center , I am integrating multisensor geolocator data with satellite imagery to investigate how arrival and departure decisions throughout a bird’s migratory journey relate to seasonal changes in plant growth. Scientists have now tracked dozens of bird species with multisensor geolocators , and that number increases every year. Each mapped migratory journey improves our understanding of how small birds migrate, what factors shape their movements, and how best to protect them. Αποτελείται από 478.000 εκτάρια…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The Great Koala National Park might sound like a place that’s too good to be true, but it is real. After more than a decade of campaigning, three state elections, and over 14 hours of parliamentary debate, New South Wales has established the state’s second-largest national park. It’s made up of 478,000 hectares (about 1.2 million acres) between Kempsey and Grafton on the Mid North Coast. More than 100 species of flora and fauna will be protected within its boundaries. The park is a patchwork of existing protected areas stitched together with more than 178,000 hectares (roughly 440,000 acres) of former state forest and Crown Land. The legislation passed through approximately 160 amendments before it got there. The campaign started small. Conservationist Ashley Love began lobbying for the park after hearing from local residents that koalas in the region weren’t as common as they once were. “It became too much to ignore,” he said. What started as a proposal to protect Crown Land eventually became a Labor election platform. NSW Labor took it to the 2015 and 2019 elections, lost both, and won government in 2023 on a ticket that included the park. Carbon credits sealed the deal Carbon credits were central to making the legislation work. The federal Clean Energy Regulator registered a project covering more than 117,000 hectares (about 289,000 acres) of the park’s state forest areas. By formally ending native forest logging there, the government can now sell carbon credits from the land. Protected forest , it turns out, generates more revenue than logged timber. Of course, that trade-off still has real costs. The Forestry Corporation of NSW had already cut more than 30 jobs in Coffs Harbour as the logging moratorium ate into forward orders. Timber NSW president Andrew Hurford laid it out: “Staff have been laid off; engineering firms that provide support to those companies have no forward orders … downstream people supplying tyres, fuel, trucking, transport, engineering. All of those things are gradually becoming slower and quieter.” The government has committed to moving displaced Forestry Corporation staff into roles with the National Parks and Wildlife Service. A park with gaps still to close NSW Environment Minister Penny Sharpe called it “a defining moment for conservation in NSW,” and by the numbers, it qualifies. Love, whose decade of advocacy made the proposal viable, was more measured. “Its nature is quite fragmented, and there are gaps and connectivity issues between sections of it, but it is a big step forward,” he said. Koalas need connected habitat to move, breed, and survive disease pressure. A 478,000-hectare patchwork is still a meaningful step up from what existed. The carbon credit structure gives the protected land a financial rationale that most past conservation campaigns lacked entirely. Love says he’ll keep pushing for the sections that didn’t make it in. After a decade, that sounds less like frustration than a habit he’s not planning to break. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: J ust weeks after conservative activist Charlie Kirk was assassinated while speaking at a college last September, students gathered in a University of Michigan classroom to discuss freedom of speech. Sitting in a semicircle, they were listening to one another share their views when one of the attendees pulled a red MAGA hat from his bag and asked if it would be okay to wear it. The gesture could have turned into a confrontation. The discussion’s moderator, however, said he was free to put it on. “We were all just like, ‘Okay, that’s your belief [and] that’s totally fine,’” recalls Sarah-Catherine Jackson, the president of BridgeUSA at UMich, the organization hosting the meeting. Students participate in a workshop at the BridgeUSA annual summit. Courtesy of BridgeUSA BridgeUSA at UMich is the University of Michigan’s chapter of BridgeUSA, a student movement built around structured political dialogue, welcoming different views as long as they are expressed with basic respect. Instead of debating for a quick win, students explain their beliefs, listen to others and stay in the room without needing to reach agreement. The need for such spaces is clear, says BridgeUSA. A 2024 Knight Foundation-Ipsos study of more than 1,500 college students between the ages of 18 and 24 found that two in three said they self-censored on topics such as gender, religion, race and LGBTQ+ issues during classroom discussions. A similar proportion reported that they believed such self-censorship limited educationally valuable conversations on campus. With another tense election pulling the country in opposite directions, BridgeUSA is betting that depolarization starts with something simple: getting supposed rivals to sit down and actually hear each other out. BridgeUSA — which was founded in 2017 at UC Berkeley after protests over a conservative speaker turned violent — works to facilitate those conversations. The organization has grown rapidly, from that first chapter in 2017, to 24 by 2020 , to 146 today. At its national summit in Philadelphia this August, 250 students gathered for leadership and moderation training, and to connect with peers from different regions and political perspectives. In spring 2024, pro-Palestine protests erupted at Columbia University in New York, leading to intensified disputes over campus speech, safety and protest, and prompting some to ask whether students with opposing views should engage with one another at all. BridgeUSA CEO Manu Meel says that when the protests began, BridgeUSA only had a small presence at the university and no trained student leaders able to convene a dialogue. But a group of students believed that kind of conversation was sorely needed, so they established a BridgeUSA chapter and organized a discussion about Israel and Palestine, an event Meel says university administrators declined to support because they feared negative publicity. The students proceeded anyway, and within a year Bridge Columbia convened a gathering of at least 200 students. While considered successful, this experience highlighted BridgeUSA’s dependence on local leadership. BridgeUSA now emphasizes trying to support rapid-response dialogue immediately after campus violence, protests and other flashpoints where possible. Listening to political opponents takes courage on campuses where students feel pressure to demonstrate ideological loyalty, says Meel, adding: “I don’t think protest is any more courageous because everybody protests today.” Instead, he describes structured dialogue as “the new campus counterculture.” Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] While dialogue performs a distinct democratic function, says University of Virginia professor Rachel Wahl, who studies political dialogue, she is wary of setting conversation and protest against each other and asserts that public demonstration remains vital: “People who want to be in dialogue should consider protest an important form of political communication.” BridgeUSA plans to grow to 800 chapters (roughly a quarter of U.S. colleges) — a reach Meel says could help make dialogue a campus norm and give quieter students “social permission” to participate. To truly make an impact, Nicholas V. Longo, director of the Rutgers Democracy Lab, asserts that dialogue must also extend into the places and spaces where students already spend time. “Campuses need to not only engage students who are ready, but also students who might avoid these kinds of opportunities. We sometimes say we want to try to make engagement in dialogue unavoidable. To do this, we need to go to where students are at — in student centers, res life and first year experiences; but then also it’s essential to build these opportunities into the curriculum.” BridgeUSA CEO Manu Meel describes structured dialogue as the new campus counterculture. Courtesy of BridgeUSA Back at the University of Michigan, where chapter meetings typically draw 10 to 15 students, keeping conversations balanced takes deliberate effort. Jackson, a self-described fairly conservative student on a predominantly liberal campus, says executive board members with different political views review presentations and social posts for partisan framing, and flag language that appears to lean left or right. The midterms bring national stakes to Ann Arbor, the home of the university, where student turnout could help shape the outcome of the state’s competitive Senate race — and, with it, which party controls the chamber. But the measure of BridgeUSA’s success extends beyond election day, says Longo, who states that dialogue can build civic knowledge and lead to informed action. After the votes are counted, it can also help students “repair and rebuild” their communities, and work together, regardless of who wins. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Sensory Food Education for Children in UK Schools Helps Pupils Enjoy Vegetables Reading Time: 3 minutes Sensory food education for children in UK schools and nurseries is fully funded, helping pupils learn to enjoy fruit and vegetables. The charity TastEd now fully funds sensory food education for children in UK schools and nurseries. It helps pupils learn to enjoy fruit and vegetables. Teachers need no kitchen or fancy equipment. The need is clear. In the UK, 79.1% of children aged 5 to 10 eat fewer than 3.5 portions of fruit and vegetables a day. In a class of 30 pupils, that is about 24 children. Put another way, only about 21% of children in that age group reach 3.5 portions. TastEd wants to change that through food lessons, using sensory food education for children in UK schools nationwide. The charity is registered in England and Wales and in Scotland. Pressure has not solved the problem. TastEd says cajoling, reward charts and 5-a-day messages have not raised intake. The 5-a-day message urges 5 portions of fruit and vegetables daily. Yet the average UK child eats just over 1 portion of vegetables a day. Why do children eat so few? TastEd points to a simple reason. Many children dislike vegetables and don’t know them well. The charity shares telling examples. It says some British 11-year-olds have never tried a raw tomato. Some 8-year-olds cannot recognize an onion. Sensory food education for children in UK schools, as delivered by teachers, is simple in practice. A teacher brings fresh fruit or vegetables into the classroom. Children talk and write about what they see, smell, touch, hear and taste. Children also say whether they enjoy the food. The setting is fun and pressure-free. TastEd says pupils often surprise themselves by enjoying foods they expected to dislike. TastEd calls taste education food education in its simplest form. It says the effect on children can be large. A course of lessons builds a taste for healthy foods and confidence in sharing preferences. Sensory food education for children in UK schools is simple in practice: a teacher brings in fresh fruit or vegetables, and children talk and write about what they see, smell, touch, hear, and taste in a fun, pressure-free setting. Photo by Yuliia Patrikhalkina on Pexels. The lessons follow the Sapere method. Many European countries have used it for decades. Evidence from Finland suggests children who receive taste education are more likely to try new vegetables, fruits and berries. The World Health Organization (WHO) backs a whole-school approach to healthy food. Its January 2026 guideline says healthy food in schools can help children build good eating habits for life. WHO estimates that 466 million children worldwide receive school meals. That fits the idea behind sensory food education for children in UK schools. Healthy habits begin early, and school is a practical place to start. Parents know the struggle. TastEd notes that giving children positive exposure to fruit and vegetables at home can be hard, especially with picky eaters. School lessons offer that exposure in a group setting. Schools also report that pupils become more adventurous with school lunches. That is a practical benefit for schools and families. Teachers get support, training and resources for sensory food education for children in UK schools. The lessons match the English National Curriculum and cover the food requirements of primary design and technology. They can also link to English, history and science. TastEd says the lessons need very few resources and no specialist knowledge. Any teacher can run them. The charity says its approach delivers the recommendations of the National Food Strategy, an independent review of England’s food system. Teachers share positive results. A reception teacher in Cambridge says the lessons build literacy skills and motivate pupils to write. A Lincolnshire teacher describes reluctant eaters becoming willing tasters over time. TastEd also explains why it is needed. It describes a worldwide child health crisis linked largely to diet. Fresh food can be costly, and some homes lack proper cooking facilities. The charity also notes that sugary foods are heavily marketed, while fresh home-made food is not. Classroom lessons give every participating child a chance to meet fresh produce. Parents and nurseries can join in too. Families can try at home with activities, lessons, and videos on the website. Activity clubs and childminders also have log-in options. Nurseries can use a dedicated page for the Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS). EYFS is the framework for children from birth to age five in England. Primary schools have their own page. Other places are seeing similar results from fresh food in school. A statewide farm-to-school program in California now reaches 500 school districts and is a permanent policy. At one district, students line up for unfamiliar fruits such as rambutan. Primary schools and nurseries can sign up for sensory food education through the TastEd website. Access is fully funded. TastEd compares taste education to learning to read and write. It calls the skill food literacy, which helps children feel confident around food. What could sensory food education for children in UK schools change if every child learned it early? The post Sensory Food Education for Children in UK Schools Helps Pupils Enjoy Vegetables appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: A journalist spent the last year of his dying father's life doing what he had always done with strangers but never with the man who had hurt him most: asking real questions and listening without flinching. What he uncovered -- in recorded conversations, old photographs, and two weathered shoeboxes hidden in plain sight -- was a pattern of compounding grief, passed quietly from generation to generation: a boy who lost his father to a war, who then couldn't be a father, who raised a son he couldn't understand. "It's the kind of wound I now see can be passed, from generation to generation, from father to son," the writer reflects. The most devastating discovery came after his father died, when he opened the shoeboxes his father had begged him to burn -- love letters from a grandfather killed in Italy in 1944, full of tender plans for a boy he would never come home to raise. What the son found there wasn't an excuse for the distance between them, but something more rare: a reason, which turned out to be enough.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Global Soil Restoration Movement Reaches 4 Billion People Across 193 Nations Reading Time: 3 minutes A global soil restoration movement, launched through a 30,000-kilometer motorcycle journey, has reached an estimated 4 billion people and is pushing nations toward policies that protect agricultural soil from irreversible degradation. Save Soil , the movement behind this global push, centers on a stark warning: soil with insufficient organic content essentially turns to sand, triggering cascading consequences for food security, water systems, biodiversity, and climate stability. Currently, 52% of agricultural soils worldwide are classified as degraded, a figure that underscores the urgency behind what has become one of the largest environmental awareness campaigns in recent history. The soil restoration movement was founded by Indian yogi and environmental activist Sadhguru, who embarked on a 100-day motorcycle journey spanning 27 countries and 30,000 kilometers from the United Kingdom to India to raise awareness. That journey became the foundation for a campaign claiming to have reached 4 billion people, roughly 60% of the world’s electorate, through 691 events and interviews, more than 8,970 media stories, and 50 iconic landmarks illuminated worldwide in support of the cause. At the core of the soil restoration movement is a specific, measurable goal: restoring at least 3% to 6% organic matter in agricultural soil by shading land and enriching it with plant litter and animal waste. The movement outlines a three-pronged policy strategy presented at the UN Convention to Combat Desertification’s COP15: incentivizing farmers to increase soil organic matter, making carbon credits more accessible to farming communities, and establishing preferential marketing for produce grown in healthier, higher-organic-matter soil. The soil restoration movement aims to restore 3% to 6% organic matter in agricultural soil, which can hold up to 90% of its weight in water, addressing a crisis in which 52% of agricultural soils worldwide are already degraded. Photo by Tom Fisk on Pexels. The stakes extend across multiple interconnected crises. Degraded soils cannot adequately absorb and regulate water flows, contributing to droughts and floods alike, while organic-rich soil can hold up to 90% of its weight in water and release it gradually over time. Soil also stores roughly three times more carbon than living plants and twice as much as the atmosphere, meaning continued degradation risks releasing roughly 850 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide, more than three decades of combined global emissions. The soil restoration movement has secured formal commitments from national governments through Soil Health memoranda of understanding, with countries including Azerbaijan, Romania, Antigua and Barbuda, Barbados, Suriname, Dominica, St. Lucia, St. Kitts and Nevis, Guyana, and the United Arab Emirates signing agreements committing to policies restoring and safeguarding soil health. The Caribbean region, in particular, has shown unified support, with multiple island nations joining within the same campaign cycle. Across North America, the soil restoration movement gained traction at the municipal level, with more than 150 cities proclaiming March 21 as Save Soil Day, including Washington, D.C., Austin, San Diego, Baltimore, Philadelphia, Phoenix, and dozens of smaller municipalities across the United States and Canada. These proclamations, while largely symbolic, reflect growing local government engagement with soil health as a civic priority rather than a purely agricultural concern. International institutions have also voiced support. The United Nations Environment Programme, the Food and Agriculture Organization, the World Health Organization, the World Food Programme, and the International Union for Conservation of Nature have all publicly backed the soil restoration movement’s objectives, alongside the Inter-American Institute for Cooperation on Agriculture and the Commonwealth of Nations. The campaign explicitly compares itself to a previous global environmental success story: the 1987 Montreal Protocol, through which 197 countries agreed to phase out ozone-depleting chemicals after confirming the Antarctic ozone hole. That agreement eliminated 99% of ozone-depleting substances, and current projections suggest the ozone layer will fully recover by mid-century. The soil restoration movement positions this precedent as proof that coordinated international policy can reverse seemingly intractable environmental crises when sufficient public and governmental will exists. Beyond policy advocacy, the soil restoration movement has catalogued more than 1,000 sustainable soil management solutions spanning 193 nations, alongside engaging younger generations directly, with 3 million children reportedly writing letters to their national leaders advocating for soil health policies. Recent reporting connected to the movement has also highlighted soil degradation’s role as a driver of global migration, with projections suggesting human displacement could double by the century’s end as soil degradation, climate change, and food insecurity compound one another. Land-related conflicts have already played a significant role in most major wars across Africa since 1990, underscoring how soil health intersects with geopolitical stability far beyond agricultural productivity alone. As the soil restoration movement continues expanding its policy reach, its core argument remains consistent: thriving soil policies require public support, and public support requires sustained awareness. Whether this translates into a binding international framework like the one that reversed ozone depletion remains to be seen, but the scale of global engagement so far suggests soil health has moved from a niche agricultural concern to a mainstream environmental and public health priority. The post Global Soil Restoration Movement Reaches 4 Billion People Across 193 Nations appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM California just gave apartment renters a shot at solar. Governor Gavin Newsom signed a bill legalizing plug-in solar panels, also called balcony solar, clearing the way for a technology that doesn’t require a roof you own, a contractor, or tens of thousands of dollars up front. Compliant models are expected to hit shelves in mid-2027. How the hardware works The hardware is minimal: a few small panels, an inverter, and cables. The panels can hang from a balcony railing, mount outside a window, or sit in a backyard. Existing models run from $300 to $2,200 , much cheaper than a rooftop installation because you set them up yourself. In Germany , where they’re already common, you just plug them into a wall outlet. California’s version has more certification requirements for now, but that’s where the law is pointed. Who is historically left out of rooftop solar? Rooftop solar has always had prerequisites. You need to own your home, have a qualifying roof, and either have capital or qualify for financing. That locked out renters from day one, along with a lot of low-income households and anyone in a multifamily building. “These small, easy-to-use solar panels will give everyone, including renters, the relief they desperately need on our outrageous energy bills,” said state Senator Scott Wiener, who wrote the bill. It passed with bipartisan support. The benefits of plug-in A plug-in system can cover up to 20 percent of a home’s electricity needs and save as much as $500 a year for a small apartment. California electric bills have climbed hard over the past few years, so that number means something to a lot of people. The registration overhaul The registration change matters nearly as much as the legalization. Under the old rules, adding a plug-in panel meant completing the same interconnection paperwork required for a full rooftop system, which could cost up to $800 and take days. Advocates noted that process cost more than the panels themselves in some cases. Under the new law, registration is free and immediate. Systems must stay under 1,200 watts per home, pass third-party safety certification, and include protection against backfeeding electricity into the grid during outages. Products currently on the market don’t meet those standards yet, so the old registration process still applies for now. The sale of non-compliant systems becomes illegal in 2030, and the law runs from 2027 to January 1, 2030. “The market is sending a clear signal to manufacturers that they need to develop a California system,” said Cora Stryker, co-founder of Bright Saver, a plug-in solar advocacy group. California is the tenth state to pass this kind of law. Utah went first in March 2025; Colorado, Virginia, and Maine followed. But California is the country’s largest electricity market, which means manufacturers pay attention in a different way. What advocates have been describing for years, plug-in solar on the shelf at a hardware store, is now a reasonable near-term prospect. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The Italian federation of pediatricians designed a box of games to help parents ask their kids how their day went. Let’s think about this for a minute. A medical organization had to build a conversation starter for families at dinner because something else kept stealing away everyone’s attention. Fifteen restaurants across Sardinia are running a one-month pilot called A tavola senza schermi , “at the table without screens.” Families who come in are asked to put their phones away. In exchange, staff hand over a “reunion kit,” a pediatrician-designed box with games, drawings, and prompts for parents and kids to work through together. The thinking behind the program The scheme is the work of Anna Cau, Sardinia’s children’s ombudsman, a former juvenile magistrate who partnered with the island’s restaurant federation to make it happen. The 15 restaurants joined voluntarily. Ultimately, the plan is to expand on the same basis. Cau is deliberate about how she describes the initiative. “The idea is not to rely solely on prohibitions or to place the burden of responsibility entirely on parents, but to ensure our broader environment supports parents in their role and helps minors integrate with others,” she said. The usual framing for children’s screen time puts the entirety of the problem on parents: their choices, their habits , their failures, their job to fix. Cau is coming at this issue from a different, more holistic angle. She wants the places families actually move through to be part of the answer rather than indifferent to the question. What restaurant owners notice Emanuele Frongia, president of the Sardinian restaurant federation, described what pushed the conversation forward. Families come in and sit down together, but within a few minutes, the talking stops. “We increasingly observe that during these moments lively chatter is replaced with stretches of silence as people look at their devices,” he said. “Often a child is handed one to keep them quiet.” It’s that last part that we really need to sit with and consider. The phone at the family table isn’t always something a kid reaches for. In fact, sometimes it’s a parent who puts it in their hands. The table in Italy isn’t just where you eat. It’s where the work of being a family gets done: the catching up, the arguing, the unremarkable talking that makes people feel known to each other. What Cau and the restaurant owners around her are watching is that shift happening meal by meal, as the phone becomes easier to reach for than whatever the silence might turn into. The real power of the reunion kit The reunion kit is both the sweetest part of this initiative and the most honest. It’s a concession that stepping away from screens needs a little structure to start. Most families handed a box of games by a waiter will end up talking without consulting the instructions. The box matters because without it, the phones inevitably come back out, at least for now. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: In an Oct. 28 letter from the editors , Life Magazine — which was founded in 1936 and became an icon of visual storytelling — announced it will begin publishing again after nearly 20 years. Its first new print issue “offers a window into an America searching for meaning.” That 250-page edition hits newsstands Nov. 23, The New York Times reported , the inaugural step forward in a revival made possible by Bedford Media’s acquisition of the publication in 2024. The holding company was founded the year prior by model Karlie Kloss and is co-owned by her husband, venture capitalist Joshua Kushner. More than 120 people put together the forthcoming issue, focusing on “finding the ordinary in the extraordinary, and the extraordinary in the ordinary,” per the editors’ letter. The reincarnated brand will expand into other avenues as well, amplifying its quarterly print pieces through digital storytelling, documentaries, and events. © CORBIS—Corbis/Getty Images When Henry Luce founded Life , at the tail end of the Great Depression and three years before World War II began, the intent was to “harness the emerging power of photojournalism,” the letter reads. Luce had co-created Time magazine 13 years prior to deliver a concise weekly news digest to busy readers. Life took an opposite approach, inviting Americans to pore over dramatic multi-page photo spreads and essays that told stories about 20th-century topics large and small: from groundbreaking science and civil rights to movie stars and the lives of everyday people. The first issue came out Nov. 23, 1936 ( you can scroll through it in its entirety online ). The cover story captured one of the major public works projects in development under then-President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s historic New Deal, and Page 2 featured a photo of a baby held upside down by a doctor moments after birth. RELATED: Gordon Parks: How Life Magazine’s First Black Staff Photographer Shed Light on Social Justice With Expressive Images That view into the miracle of life (no pun intended) likely felt unprecedented to readers at the time. The newborn was George Story, who went on to become a journalist and liked to joke at parties that a nude picture of him had once been published in a national magazine. Santi Visalli/Getty Images After nearly four decades, Time Inc. ceased weekly publication of Life in 1972, citing production costs. The magazine returned in 1978 as a monthly publication and ran until 2000. In a full-circle moment, its final issue in that format also featured Story — this time covering his death at age 63. It was resurrected again in 2004 as a weekly newspaper supplement, but shut down three years later due to a decline in newspaper readership and ad sales, the company said, per NBC News. The upcoming revival marks exactly 90 years since Life began. Take a look back at some of its most iconic photos and covers. items.description: Κάπου ανάμεσα στα φαράγγια και τους βοτανικούς κήπους της πανεπιστημιούπολης του Πανεπιστημίου Cornell, ένας φοιτητής σε μια καθοδηγούμενη βόλτα στη φύση σήκωσε το βλέμμα του μετά από ώρες οθόνης και είπε κάτι που εμπόδισε τον αρχηγό της περιπάτου να είναι ψυχρή: «Είναι η πρώτη φορά που αγγίζω γρασίδι». Ήταν μια μικρή ομολογία, αλλά έφερε το βάρος μιας επιδημίας. Σε όλες τις πανεπιστημιουπόλεις των ΗΠΑ,…
items.descriptionOriginal: Somewhere between the gorges and botanic gardens of Cornell University's campus, a student on a guided nature walk looked up from hours of screen time and said something that stopped the walk leader cold: "This is the first time I've actually touched grass." It was a small confession, but it carried the weight of an epidemic. Across U.S. campuses, colleges are turning to "social prescribing" -- a practice borrowed from the UK where physicians write actual referrals, logged in electronic health records, for time in nature, art, movement, or community -- as a complement to counseling and medication for the surging mental health crisis among students. At Cornell, over 2,200 students received nature prescriptions last year, and 88 percent reported an improved mood. At Stanford, a dedicated care navigator connects students to pottery classes, dance workshops, and live performances -- and 80 percent of those who attended reported better mental health. What these programs are quietly surfacing is something older than any diagnosis: that belonging, beauty, and the sensory world are not luxuries but medicine. The student who finally touched grass wasn't being dramatic. She was describing a kind of return.

items.descriptionOriginal: Do you tend to experience jealousy, have difficulty trusting people, or resist emotional intimacy out of fear? While genetics can play a role in qualities like these presenting themselves, they may also be explained by attachment theory: the idea that our earliest relationships influence how we’ll connect with people later in life. “As children, we build our understanding of relationships based on our caregivers,” Jennifer Rolnick , a licensed clinical psychologist and co-owner of Watch Hill Therapy, told Nice News. “If a caregiver is consistently supportive, a child learns that relationships are safe. If a caregiver is inconsistent, distant, or intimidating, a child learns defense mechanisms in order to survive.” These early, deeply ingrained patterns shape how we read people, manage conflict, and regulate emotions, resulting in specific “attachment styles” that we hold onto into adulthood, Rolnick explained. Those of us with a secure attachment style usually find it easier to nurture and sustain close connections, while those with insecure attachment styles (avoidant, anxious, or disorganized) often have trouble in adult relationships. But the good news is that it’s entirely possible to change your patterns. We spoke to Rolnick and three other experts to help us understand the four attachment styles, including how they develop and what you can do to form more secure relationship habits with friends, family, and romantic partners moving forward. Understanding the 4 Attachment Styles Avoidant We might develop an avoidant attachment style if our primary caregiver was emotionally distant or dismissive, per Utah State University . This attachment style can also occur if we were regularly and unreasonably depended on or criticized as a child, Hider Shaaban , a licensed clinical psychologist and founding executive director of Philadelphia Center for Psychotherapy, told Nice News. “So [they] may develop a core belief of ‘If I let people get close to me, they will drain me, judge me, and maybe even hurt me along the way, so it’s safer that I keep my distance.’” Adults with avoidant attachment styles prioritize independence and self-reliance over close connection, added Terri DiMatteo , a licensed professional counselor at Open Door Therapy. “Deep emotional intimacy or vulnerability feels uncomfortable to them,” she said. “When a romantic or non-romantic person gets too close, they are likely to pull away and create distance. Avoidantly attached adults have great difficulty expressing their own emotions, and in the back of their mind is the refrain ‘I don’t need anyone. I am good on my own.’” fizkes—iStock/Getty Images Plus According to the Cleveland Clinic , other potential signs of avoidant attachment include: A strong sense of independence Difficulty trusting people Avoiding physical or emotional intimacy Feeling uncomfortable when people try to get close Being dismissive of others Commitment issues Anxious If you had an inconsistent or emotionally unpredictable caregiver, you might have developed an anxious attachment style, explained Emily Bly , a licensed clinical psychologist and CEO of Psychology Partners Group. When parents “are particularly inconsistent in their emotional responses — vacillating between warm and connected at some moments and cold, nonresponsive, and detached in other moments — [it] can result in the child internalizing a sense that they are ‘not good enough’ or to blame in some way.” Bly added that people with anxious attachment styles tend to fear abandonment and worry that a loved one could withdraw their affection at any time and without warning. They frequently seek reassurance and have trouble believing that people really care for them, and are often on high alert for potential signs of dismissal or rejection. For instance, they might interpret a partner’s subtle shift in tone or a friend’s delayed text response as a signal that something is wrong in the relationship. According to the Cleveland Clinic, signs of anxious attachment include: Feeling unworthy of love Difficulty spending time alone High sensitivity to criticism Jealous tendencies Low self-esteem Trouble trusting people Fear of abandonment or rejection Disorganized A disorganized attachment style (also known as fearful avoidant) can occur if a primary caregiver is dangerous or violent. If a parent consistently frightens a child, the child has nowhere to turn in times of distress, Bly explained. As a result, they may develop a “freeze” response to emotional turmoil, feeling that they can’t escape or rely upon their parent. In adulthood, they may shut down and “quasi-dissociate” when stressed, making it difficult for someone else to reach them emotionally, she continued. Relationships can therefore be confusing, as it may feel like the fearful avoidant-attached person has one foot on the gas and another on the brakes. Igor Suka—E+/Getty Images “A person with disorganized attachment craves security and attachment like anyone else, but the fear embedded in this longing will sometimes put the person in a state of ‘system overload,’” Bly said, “where they might be more likely to disappear or ‘ghost’ the attachment figure who tries to get too close to them.” According to the Cleveland Clinic, signs of disorganized attachment include: Difficulty trusting others Trouble with emotional regulation Fear of rejection Confusing, contradictory behaviors Other traits of anxious and avoidant attachments Secure When caregivers provide consistent predictability, abundant love, clear expectations, and straightforward communication, children are often more likely to develop secure attachments. “Basically, they will start to develop the belief system that ‘relationships are generally safe,’ which will help them establish connections with others without the worry of being rejected,” Shaaban said. When they do experience rejection, he added, they’re less likely to take it personally and can bounce back more quickly. People with secure attachment typically view themselves and others positively, communicate honestly and openly, and find it easier to build and maintain lasting, healthy bonds, according to Utah State University. DiMatteo agreed: “Securely attached relationships are safe, relaxed, reliable, and supportive, allowing each person to be their authentic self, knowing they are accepted and valued as they are.” According to the Cleveland Clinic, signs of secure attachment include: Finding it easy to trust others Effective communication Emotional regulation Feeling comfortable spending time alone Finding it easy to connect with others Healthy conflict resolution Being emotionally available to other people How to Become More Secure If you’re prone to forming avoidant, anxious, or disorganized attachments, you can develop an “earned secure” attachment style through healthy adult relationships, positive life experiences, and working with a therapist, per the Cleveland Clinic . Seeing a mental health professional experienced in attachment theory and relationships is especially important if you have a history of trauma, Shaaban noted. You can also try the following to develop healthier, more secure relationship patterns. Understand Your Story: Think about your early childhood and how you developed an insecure attachment style, Bly said. Recognize that your caregiver’s faults, such as inconsistency or emotional distance, reflect their own struggles and have nothing to do with you. With that knowledge, you can begin to rewrite your internal narrative and develop a healthier view of yourself and other people. Seek Out Stable, Secure Relationships: “Be purposeful about seeking out and establishing connections with people who are emotionally mature, consistent, and grounded,” DiMatteo advised. Observing and interacting with securely attached people — including friends, a romantic partner, or a therapist — can help you understand what healthy relationship patterns look like, aiding you in eventually adopting similar behaviors. andreswd—E+/Getty Images Identify Your Triggers: Note the situations that activate your emotional defense mechanisms. “Track your thoughts, bodily sensations, and immediate coping mechanisms when triggered,” Rolnick said. “Writing down your patterns helps you understand yourself rather than running on autopilot.” Practice Honest, Open Communication: Secure attachment involves clear, direct, and authentic interactions with others, and Rolnick suggests working on this by sharing a vulnerable feeling or need with someone you trust once a week. “Vulnerability means something different for every person, and it’s important to gently push your window of tolerance. You might say ‘I felt anxious when I didn’t hear back from you for a few days,’ or ‘I’m having a hard day and feeling anxious — can we talk?’ Each time you face your fear directly, you build your ability to handle similar challenges in the future.” RELATED: Dealing With a Difficult Relationship? Here’s How Psychology Says You Can Shift the Dynamic

items.descriptionOriginal: For 39 years, Marilyn Hampton swept floors, bought supplies for children who couldn't afford them, and turned smiles "up instead of down" -- work she once measured against a college degree she never earned and found herself wanting. The custodian who privately carried a sense of failure was, to everyone around her, the living heart of Aubrey Independent School District in Texas. When the superintendent called her to the podium under the pretense of a routine meeting, Hampton unrolled a small red carpet and found her own name printed on it: Marilyn Hampton Elementary School. The next day, she was still crying. "Whoever thought a janitor would have a school named after them," she said, and in that sentence lives the quiet revelation the story holds: that a life spent in faithful, unglamorous service to others can quietly become the most significant thing in a room, in a district, in a community's memory -- long before anyone thinks to say so out loud.

items.descriptionOriginal: In the second half of Stanley Kubrick’s The Shining , there’s an iconic sequence that’s arguably as terrifying as Jack Nicholson’s ax-wielding rampage. It begins quietly, the camera following Shelley Duvall as she walks toward a shadowy room. Her footsteps echo in the silence before an ominous sound creeps in, almost like distorted white noise. The music builds, getting louder and more complex as warped high notes slowly penetrate the din. It’s chaotic, dissonant, deafening, mirroring the emotions on Duvall’s face, until finally, finally — well, we won’t give you any spoilers . “If you watched it on mute, I don’t know if it would feel nearly as scary,” Rock Burwell told Nice News of the classic flick. Burwell composed the score for this year’s breakout indie horror film, Obsession , which raked in $500 million-plus off a $750,000 budget, making it the highest-grossing movie ever produced for under $1 million. The Los Angeles-based composer recognizes how essential music is to evoking emotion in filmgoers, and his eerie orchestration played an outsize role in Obsession’s success. “What just generally has always drawn me to music in the first place is its ability to influence how we feel,” he said. But what exactly makes scary music scary? We may all have some general idea of the characteristics of creepy music — the crescendo of staccato strings in Psycho ’s shower scene comes to mind — but the way in which a score achieves its effect varies greatly. There are certain common elements, however, that lend themselves to disconcerting an audience. Subverting Expectations For Obsession , Burwell — after discussions with writer-director Curry Barker — chose a nontraditional approach, opting to subtly discomfit viewers through dreamy, nostalgic melodies, slightly pitch-bending his notes and drenching everything in reverb. “It was fun to explore not coming in with these really harsh, interval, screechy-sounding kind of things that you hear in a lot of horror movies,” he explained, “but actually coming from something that feels a bit more warm and almost comforting. But the way it moves and is undulating underneath is very — it kind of gets under your skin a little bit more.” Composer Katy Jarzebowski , who recently scored the award-winning documentary Gaslit featuring Jane Fonda, has been working in the industry for over 20 years. She noted that today’s savvy audiences are well-versed in the language of film. The key to unsettling them, then, is to present a musical choice they don’t necessarily understand or expect. “If you give them something that they know and love, then it kind of takes that feeling of discomfort away,” she explained, adding: “[When filmmakers] don’t give them something that they expect, it becomes uncomfortable.” Tension Tension is the heart of any horror film, and a good one typically leaves viewers on tenterhooks throughout. To that end, Burwell noted that the descending melodies and drawn-out cues he used can cause audiences to feel as though they’re suspended, waiting for a resolution that never comes. “Everything is very, like, ambient and long, and it’s slow moving,” he said. “I think that the pace of it really allows those feelings to sit in a bit longer.” He added that he’s heard from fans that the sweet-yet-tainted score had them feeling “very comforted, but at the same time, feeling kind of bad or that there’s something missing or that there’s yearning.” Jarzebowski agreed with the idea of holding out on viewers. “It’s a lot about where you choose to come in or where you choose to hold back,” she said. “You know, a lot of times [it’s] not giving that kind of pillow for the audience to land on to remind them that they’re in a movie in the first place.” In the Studio Pete Horner is an Emmy-winning sound designer and re-recording mixer at Skywalker Sound (who also happens to be married to Jarzebowski). He pointed out that the terror conveyed through a horror movie’s sound isn’t merely from the music itself. Foley is the art of creating sound effects in a studio — things like footsteps or a door creaking — and Horner said it can be used to great effect for inducing fear in quiet scenes. “By accentuating those things, it kind of draws you closer to the action, and it makes you feel uncomfortable because you shouldn’t be able to hear that,” he explained, adding: “It mimics what happens when you are scared, which is that you become hyperaware of your surroundings. And when you’re not scared, you probably don’t hear the footsteps at all, even though they are happening in the space you’re in. But if you are scared, every little tiny sound has huge meaning.” Additionally, gradually removing the ambient background noise (called “room tone”) from a scene can be extremely disconcerting. “It’s something you want to use sparingly in a movie, but if you pull out of all of the ambiences, the effect that it has is the audience will hold their breath,” Horner said. “Because they’re listening, they’re trying to hear into the sound, and there’s nothing there. And it’s a very scary feeling.” Working With the Cinematography It’s typical for musicians to score to picture, meaning they create the music as they watch the film. But sometimes, the two arts inform each other more equally. In Obsession , Burwell sent early cues to Barker while he and director of photography Taylor Clemons were coming up with the shot list. Barker later told Burwell that playing the music on set really helped establish the mood they were going for. Likewise, watching Clemons’ claustrophobic cinematography influenced Burwell’s choices for the score. “We kind of leaned on the darkness, like, there’s not much high frequency information in the music, and there’s not a whole lot of light in a lot of these scenes, too,” Burwell said. “I’ve kind of referred to it as a lot of the score feeling like a lead blanket or something like that. Like, it’s just really heavy. And I think the cinematography really informed that for me.” Experimentation Starting with what’s considered the first-ever horror flick (a three-minute silent French film from 1896 titled The Haunted Castle ) to the dozens coming out in 2027 , the genre is a confirmed favorite of moviegoers. Call it sublimation or call it masochism, but people like to be scared. And that means composers have ample opportunity — and one could say the imperative — to get creative. “Horror is a great place for composers, especially to experiment with different things because a lot of times, you’re trying to create a fear that someone doesn’t know yet,” Jarzebowski said, adding: “We already have Psycho , we have Stranger Things , we have [horror filmmaker and composer John] Carpenter — all this horror language that we’ve created. So you already know what to be scared of. So there’s always room for, like, ‘OK, what else can we do to make it even scarier? What haven’t they heard yet?’”

items.descriptionOriginal: What spooks you? A mysterious thud downstairs in the middle of the night, spotting a spider on your pillow, and feeling something brush against your leg in the sea are among the top 10 things that make Brits scream, according to a recent survey of 2,000 adults in the U.K. Yet despite being quick to shriek, the nation appears to embrace the fun side of fear, with 84% of respondents saying scary experiences are more likely to end in laughter than panic when shared with others. More than half also confirmed enjoying spooky thrills in a group setting tends to leave them laughing, particularly when watching horror films, riding roller coasters, or braving a haunted attraction. SWNS According to psychologist Kimberley Wilson, there’s a scientific reason these scary experiences can feel surprisingly enjoyable, something she’s dubbed the “Shared Shriek Effect.” “When we watch something scary, our bodies respond as if we’re facing a threat. Our heart rate increases, adrenaline rises, and our attention sharpens,” she told SWNS. “The difference is that our brains know we’re actually safe, which allows us to experience that physical rush as excitement rather than fear.” Wilson added: “When we share that experience with other people, whether we’re jumping, screaming, or laughing together, it can create a genuine sense of connection. The scream itself also helps release the tension that’s been building up, which is why laughter so often follows.” There are benefits beyond the thrill, too, with a quarter saying that being scared offers an escape from everyday life, while 24% see it as a healthy emotional release. Nearly 1 in 5 of those polled also believe it acts as an instant stress reliever. The research was done via OnePoll and commissioned by M&M’s to mark the launch of the candy brand’s new “ Screaming Service ,” encouraging people to swap streaming for screaming this Halloween. “We think Halloween isn’t really about being scared, it’s about screaming together,” said Georgia Woodward, a senior brand manager at M&M’s. “Our ‘Screaming Service’ celebrates those moments across the month of Halloween when everyone jumps at the same scenes, hides behind a cushion, and ends up laughing together about it afterwards.” Top 10 Things That Make Brits Shriek SWNS 1. Someone unexpectedly jumping out at you as a prank 2. Hearing a knock at the window when it’s dark 3. Hearing a mysterious thud downstairs in the night 4. Missing a step at the bottom of the stairs 5. Spotting a spider on your pillow 6. Feeling something brush against your leg in the sea 7. Seeing a mouse dart across a room 8. Being caught off guard by a spooky film twist 9. Someone unexpectedly shouting “boo!” 10. Walking face-first into a cobweb This article was originally written by Zara Zubeidi for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.
